title: API Evangelist Daily — Monday, November 2, 2026
description:
This is the API Evangelist Daily for Monday, November 2, 2026 — what is new across APIs.io, API Evangelist and API Commons, plus a few things from the shelf.

New on API Evangelist

  • Add Webhooks To Your Product And Recover Failed Deliveries With Svix — A big customer asks whether your product can notify their system the moment an order ships. Your engineers say yes, then quote you weeks of work, because sending the message turns out to be the easy part.
  • Check Two OpenAPI Versions For Breaking Changes, And Know What It Cannot See — This is the third story in my series on what each API Evangelist operation can do. Friday I searched sixteen years of research.
  • Control Who Sees Your Data, Manage Warehouses And Run AI Models With Snowflake — A new analyst starts on Monday and can't see the sales tables until someone files a request. A departing contractor still has access nobody remembered to remove.
  • Plus 6 more today: Find The Root Cause Of Outages, Search Logs And Forecast Monitoring Costs With Dynatrace; Manage Marketing Emails, Campaign Budgets And Customer Conversations With HubSpot; Run Website Reports, Send Server Events And Handle Privacy Deletion Requests With Google Analytics; The Decoder Only Pours Part Of The Bedrock; The Same Fifty Providers Sit Under Every Kind Of Application; Use A Score To Build Your API Roadmap And Not To Chase A Number

New on APIs.io

  • AI Agents has 1,016 providers and 41.0% of them are still human-only — The AI Agents tag on apis.io holds 1,016 providers and 323 APIs, and one number frames it: 417 of those providers, 41.0%, sit in the human-only band of our agent readiness measure. These are companies carrying the word agent on their own listing.
  • Four of the top 20 in our investing industry manage infrastructure, not money — Four of the 20 highest scorers in our Investing & Venture Capital industry have nothing to do with investing. Bentley Systems is fifth at 71.2, Limble CMMS seventh at 70.8, MaintainX twelfth at 66.7 and SewerAI tied for eighteenth at 63.9.
  • Infobip's Connectivity API offers SIM swap checks twice, and its async lookup has no webhook contract — The Infobip Connectivity API is the telecom identity layer of Infobip: number lookups, silent mobile verification, SIM swap checks, national ID checks, biometric sessions, and CAMARA endpoints. Its contract has 36 operations and 7 webhooks.
  • Plus 8 more today: Just over half of our pricing records cite evidence, and 32% of them were generated; Palo Alto Networks Moves Agent Identity Into Silicon. Its Record Has Not Followed.; Photoroom Says Fix the Catalog Before the Protocol, and Its Own Record Shows the Same Gap; The serverless page shows 30 of 141 providers, and the sample flatters the market by 23 points; SimScale Polled Engineers on AI, and One in Twenty Are Scaling It; Sobot Defines the Customer Service Agent Skill. Its API Pages Do Not Show One Yet.; Three times as many provider sites serve llms.txt as security.txt; A Workato Customer Says Nobody Has Figured Out Agent Pricing, So Build the Meter First

Kin Score mover

  • Sully AI rose 24.4 points, from 21.0 to 45.4 (developing), between the 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31 scoring runs.

Provider spotlight

  • Mastercard — Mastercard is a global technology company in the payments industry, providing APIs for payment processing, fraud detection, data analytics, and financial services. Kin Score 57.3 (strong), agent readiness 42.8 (agent-native).

From the conversations

  • API Evangelist Conversation with Reza Shafii, Product Executive At Kong — My friend Emanual had tagged me in one of Reza's posts on LinkedIn about API integrations being dead, so I invitied Reza to come over and explain more about what he meant. I knew the title was bait, but I was interested in hearing Reza's argument and after the conversation it is clear that he's done a lot of thinking at this intersection and wasn't just adding to the AI hype.

FAQ

  • How do I name things in my API? Use the language the business uses, plural nouns for collections, consistent casing everywhere, and no abbreviations that require a decoder ring. Then write the convention down and lint it.

Guidance

  • Quality — The measurable correctness consistency and completeness of API definitions

Standard

  • EPCIS — EPCIS (Electronic Product Code Information Services) is the GS1 standard for capturing and sharing supply chain event data — what happened to an object, where, when, and why.

Investor

  • Foundry Group — Foundry Group is a Boulder, Colorado venture capital firm founded in 2007 by Brad Feld, Seth Levine, Ryan McIntyre, and Jason Mendelson. The firm invests in early-stage technology startups across the United States, organizing its work around long-lived, horizontal investment themes (such as "glue", "protocol", "distribution", and "human computer interaction") rather than narrow verticals, with a particular affinity…

Country

  • 🇵🇹 Portugal — 10 API providers on APIs.io; the most in Artificial Intelligence (3), Customer Support & Service (2), Government & Public Sector (2).

Regulation

  • ESIGN Act and UETA — ESIGN is the US federal statute giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as their paper equivalents, and UETA is the uniform state law adopted in almost every state that does the same at state level.

Tool

  • Apache CouchDB — NoSQL document database using JSON for documents, HTTP for API, and JavaScript for MapReduce queries.

Everything mentioned is linked in the show notes. Find any API at apis.io, and see what we are working on at apievangelist.com.

title: Dev News Digest: 3 Nov 2026, 18:00
description:

Security

Platforms & tools

title: Snowflake's Always-On Bots Want to Work While You're Away — Explained Honestly
description:
Snowflake is pitching a simple idea: instead of you going to the data, always-on bots go to work for you — and keep working while you are away.

That sounds useful. It also sounds like the kind of claim that needs to be read carefully, because not everything in this announcement is available in the same way, at the same time, to everyone.

This is an honest explainer, not a buyer-intent post and not a hands-on review. No hands-on testing was performed for this article, and there are no affiliate links in it.

What is being announced, in plain terms

The central idea is autonomous work inside Snowflake: bots that can carry out ongoing data work, rather than only answering a single question when asked.

Think of it less as a chatbot you prompt once, and more as a worker you set up, give boundaries to, and then check on. The appeal is obvious: routine preparation, monitoring and follow-up that would otherwise wait for a person.

The risk is also obvious: work that continues without a person in the loop needs clear limits, clear ownership, and a clear way to see what it did and why.

The important distinction: what is GA, what is preview, and what is coming

This is where most coverage gets sloppy, so let us be precise:

  • CoCo Automations is generally available (GA). This is the part described as ready for general use.
  • Slack, Excel, Google Sheets and Mobile are in public preview. They are available to try in preview, not presented here as finished, generally available products.
  • The Snowflake CoCo / CoWork Bots are in private preview soon — NOT generally available. Do not treat them as something you can simply switch on today. “Private preview soon” means limited, forthcoming access, not general availability.

If a summary tells you all of this is simply “live now”, it is oversimplifying the announcement.

Why always-on work is different from a normal AI assistant

A normal assistant helps you in the moment. An always-on bot is supposed to help you over time.

That changes the questions you should ask:

  • What exactly is it allowed to change, and what is it only allowed to read or suggest?
  • How does it handle a task that is partly finished, ambiguous, or wrong halfway through?
  • Who is accountable when it acts while no one is watching?
  • How do you audit its work afterwards?
  • How do you pause it, roll it back, or stop it cleanly?

Until those answers are clear for your own data and workflows, “always-on” should be treated as a capability to govern, not just a feature to enable.

Adoption: read the claims as claims

Any adoption figures attached to this announcement are Snowflake's claims, not independently verified figures. That does not make them false — it means this article does not independently confirm them, and readers should not treat vendor figures as independent measurement.

The same caution applies to productivity and efficiency claims. They are interesting as signals of what Snowflake believes customers are experiencing, but they are not a substitute for testing in your own environment, with your own data, permissions and costs.

Pricing: none is stated here

No pricing is stated in this article because none was given for it. Do not infer a price, a tier, or a “free” or “included” status from this post. If pricing matters to your decision — and it should — check Snowflake's current pricing and terms directly before planning around it.

What this does not prove

To be clear about the limits of this article:

  • No hands-on testing was performed.
  • This is not a review of a product you can use today in its private-preview form.
  • This is not a recommendation to buy, migrate, or adopt anything.
  • This does not verify Snowflake's adoption claims independently.
  • This does not state pricing, because none was given.

What it does do is separate the announcement into its actual availability stages, so you are not misled by a single headline.

A practical way to think about it

If you are evaluating this kind of tool, start with a narrow, reversible use case:

  1. Pick work that is routine, well-defined and easy to check.
  2. Set tight permissions and a clear owner.
  3. Require a readable log of what the bot did.
  4. Review the results before anything affects production data or external communication.
  5. Only widen the scope after the checks have actually passed.

That approach works whether the eventual product is excellent or disappointing — and it protects you while private-preview features are still, by definition, not generally available.

The bottom line

Snowflake's always-on bots are an interesting direction: data work that does not wait for you to ask. But the honest version of the story has stages. CoCo Automations is GA. Slack, Excel, Sheets and Mobile are in public preview. The CoCo / CoWork Bots themselves are private preview soon, not generally available.

Judge the idea on that timeline — not on a headline that flattens it.

FAQ

Are Snowflake's CoCo / CoWork Bots generally available?

No. They are described as private preview soon, not generally available.

What is generally available?

CoCo Automations is GA.

What is in public preview?

Slack, Excel, Google Sheets and Mobile are in public preview.

Are the adoption figures independently verified?

No. Adoption figures in this area are Snowflake's claims, not independently verified figures.

How much does it cost?

No pricing is stated in this article because none was given. Check Snowflake's current pricing directly.

Was this hands-on tested?

No. No hands-on testing was performed for this article.

Is this a buying recommendation or an affiliate post?

No. There are no affiliate links in this article, and it is not a buyer-intent post.

title: How to Do a Reverse Face Search on a Dating Profile Photo (Step-by-Step, 2026)
description:
To reverse face search a dating photo, crop the face, then run it through a face search engine. ProfileFinder.ai checks faces against dating profiles on Tinder, Bumble and Hinge, PimEyes and Lenso.ai scan the open web, and Cheaterbuster or Social Catfish add name-based identity checks.

A plain reverse image search (Google Lens, TinEye) looks for the same picture. A face search looks for the same person, even in a different photo. That difference matters on dating apps, because scammers rarely reuse a single image. They take a whole album from someone's Instagram.

Why bother checking a profile photo

The FTC lists a reverse image search of the profile picture as one of the first steps when you suspect a romance scam: if the photo is associated with another name or with details that don't match up, that is a warning sign. Bumble's own scam guidance says the same thing in its article on protecting yourself from romance scams.

Step 1: Get the cleanest image you can

Dating apps do not let you download photos directly, so take a screenshot of the profile picture.

  • Pick the photo where the face is largest, front-facing and well lit.
  • Avoid group shots, sunglasses, heavy filters and side profiles.
  • If there are several photos, screenshot two or three. Different angles improve your chances.

Step 2: Crop to the face

Crop the screenshot so the face fills most of the frame, leaving a little hair and chin. Remove app buttons, text overlays and other people. Face engines detect the largest face first, so a tight crop prevents them from matching the wrong person.

Step 3: Run a standard reverse image search first

Upload the full, uncropped photo to Google Lens or TinEye. This catches the lazy cases: stock photos, a known influencer, or a picture already flagged on scam-warning sites. It takes thirty seconds and is free.

Step 4: Run a face search

Now upload the cropped face to a face search engine. Which one depends on your question.

Question you're asking Recommended tool What it compares against Free option
Is this face on other dating apps? ProfileFinder.ai Dating profiles (Tinder, Bumble, Hinge, Badoo, OkCupid) See site
Where else is this face online? PimEyes Public web pages Limited previews
Is this a stolen social media photo? Lenso.ai Public web images Limited searches
Does the name match the person? Social Catfish Public records and social sources Limited
Is this specific person on Tinder? Cheaterbuster Tinder profiles No

If you are vetting a match, open-web engines answer "is this photo stolen?". If you are checking whether a partner or ex has profiles elsewhere, a dating-focused engine answers "is this person also on other apps?". Many people need both.

Step 5: Read the results carefully

A face match is a lead, not a verdict. For each result, check:

  • Name and age. Do they match what the person told you?
  • Location. A match "in London" whose photos turn up on a Brazilian model's portfolio is a red flag.
  • Dates. An old blog photo is consistent with a real person; a dozen unrelated names across sites is not.
  • Similarity, not certainty. Siblings and lookalikes exist. Look for an identical background, outfit or tattoo before concluding.

Step 6: Use the app's own verification

Ask your match to verify. Tinder's Photo Verification compares a video selfie with profile photos, and Bumble's photo verification uses a selfie plus human review. Someone who refuses to verify and also won't video call is giving you an answer.

Step 7: Act on what you found

If the photos belong to someone else, stop sending personal information, report the profile in the app, and if money was involved, report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov as the FTC advises. If the search simply confirms the person is real, you've lost nothing but a few minutes.

Privacy and fair use

Face search is powerful, so use it for safety, not for tracking people who have cut contact with you. Only search photos that were shown to you, and do not share the results publicly. Tinder notes on its safety tips page that it's worth getting a vibe check before sharing personal details. The same applies in reverse: don't dig further into someone's life than meeting them safely requires.

FAQ

Can I reverse search a Tinder or Bumble photo?

Yes. Screenshot the photo, crop it to the face, and upload it to a face search engine. Open-web tools find copies elsewhere online, while ProfileFinder.ai compares the face against dating profiles on several apps.

Is reverse face search more accurate than Google Images?

For people, usually yes. Google Lens and TinEye mainly find copies of the same image. A face search engine can match the same person across different photos, which is how stolen photo sets are usually caught.

What if the face search finds nothing?

No result is mildly reassuring but not proof. The photo may be new, private, or AI-generated. Ask for Photo Verification or a short video call, which is harder to fake than a still image.

title: LLM API Pricing Compared: Claude vs GPT vs Gemini vs DeepSeek (Live Numbers, Nov 2026)
description:
Short version: the gap between a model vendor's list price and what you actually pay on a multi-seller LLM gateway can be an order of magnitude — but the deepest discount you see is the best tier available right now, not a price every request gets. Below is one table comparing official list prices against live effective prices for eight major model vendors.

Data as of 2026-11-04 00:35 (UTC+8). The platform currently tracks 352 model profiles across 49 vendors; 190 models are listed for sale right now. Prices move as sellers post and withdraw asks, so treat the live table as the source of truth.

One table: official list price vs. live effective price

Vendor Model Official (CNY / 1M tokens, in / out) Effective, deepest tier Discount Sellers
Anthropic claude-sonnet-5 13.39 / 66.95 0.603 / 3.01 0.45 折 7
OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol 26.78 / 134 0.643 / 3.21 0.24 折 11
Google gemini-3.1-pro 13.39 / 80.34 2.01 / 12.05 1.5 折 7
DeepSeek deepseek-v4-flash 2 / 8 0.2 / 0.8 1 折 6
Alibaba qwen3.8-max 12 / 36 1.2 / 3.6 1 折 6
Zhipu glm-5.3 8 / 28.01 0.8 / 2.8 1 折 7
Moonshot kimi-k3 20 / 100 2 / 10 1 折 6
MiniMax MiniMax-M3 2.1 / 8.4 0.21 / 0.84 1 折 6

Official prices are converted at 1 USD = 6.695 CNY. The effective price is computed from the deepest ask tier currently posted, so the seller count next to it matters: a 0.45 折 tier with a single seller is one seller's quote, not a market-wide price. Live price table →

How to read this table

  • Official — the vendor's public input/output price, converted to CNY.
  • Effective — official price multiplied by the deepest discount tier that sellers are currently posting for that model.
  • Discount (折) — the fraction of the official price you pay. 5 折 means half the list price; 0.45 折 means 4.5% of it. A seller may not quote more than 5 折, and the deepest tier currently allowed is 0.01 折.
  • Sellers — how many sellers currently have an ask on that model. Check the model plaza for live availability before you build on a specific tier.

Why the price is lower

This is not a single upstream reseller adding a markup. Sellers list spare model quota at their own prices, and the platform dispatches to the best available ask based on price, load and health, failing over automatically when a route dies. The discount comes from reselling idle quota, bulk purchasing and regional pricing — not from a different, weaker model. Platform commission is currently 0% while seller support is running.

Picking by workload

  • Long context / coding — Anthropic, OpenAI, Moonshot and Zhipu model pages
  • Cheapest general purpose — DeepSeek, Alibaba and MiniMax
  • Image and video generation — filter by category in the model plaza

Every model has a documentation page with its billing units, tier table and a runnable example: see model docs.

Integrating in three lines

The API is OpenAI-compatible — point base_url at the gateway and keep your existing client:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="sk-...",                      # your LONG AI key
    base_url="https://ai.dijinlong.com/v1", # OpenAI-compatible endpoint
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi"}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Billing is per-token, settled in CNY, with no plans and no minimum spend. Full setup instructions: integration docs.

FAQ

Does everyone get the deepest discount in the table? No. It is the best ask posted at the time of writing. Your actual price depends on which tier the router picks, based on availability and load.

Where does the gap between list price and effective price come from? List price is what the vendor charges. Effective price is what a seller asks for idle quota; the platform matches, routes and settles.

What if there is only one seller? Routing fails over to another seller automatically. If a model has only one seller in total, keep a comparable backup model in your fallback list.

Data notes

352 model profiles / 49 vendors; 190 models listed for sale. Profile count is not the same as listed count. Official prices converted at 1 USD = 6.695 CNY; the effective price uses the deepest tier at the time of writing, so quote the date when you cite these numbers. Full price list: ai.dijinlong.com/pricing.

Disclosure: this article is published by the LONG AI team (support@dijinlong.com). We build the platform being described, so treat the numbers as a first-party statement rather than an independent review.

title: Stop Trusting Vibes: Build a Minimal LLM Eval Harness Before You Claim Your Model Got Better
description:
Tuần này trên Hacker News có một bài hơn 580 điểm chỉ ra rằng bài viết kiểu "Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen" đang gây hiểu lầm. Mình không bàn chuyện ai đúng ai sai. Điều đáng nói là cả cộng đồng mất mấy ngày tranh cãi chỉ vì một lý do: claim "model tốt hơn" mà không có eval đủ chặt. Chuyện này không chỉ xảy ra với các lab lớn. Team mình từng merge một LoRA adapter chỉ vì "test thử 10 câu thấy ngon hơn". Hai tuần sau, khách hàng báo model trả lời sai format JSON nhiều gấp đôi. Bài này chia sẻ cách mình dựng một eval harness tối thiểu (khoảng 100 dòng Python) để mỗi lần đổi prompt, fine-tune hay đổi model, mình có con số đáng tin chứ không phải cảm giác.

Vì sao "nhìn thấy tốt hơn" không phải là bằng chứng

Có 4 cái bẫy mà mình gặp đi gặp lại:

  • Cherry-picking: bạn nhớ 3 câu model mới trả lời hay và quên 5 câu nó trả lời tệ hơn.
  • Sample size quá nhỏ: 10 câu thì chênh 1 câu đã là 10%. Mức nhiễu đó đủ lớn để bạn "thấy" cải thiện ở bất cứ đâu.
  • Variance do sampling: với temperature=0.7, cùng một câu hỏi chạy 3 lần có thể ra 3 kết quả khác nhau. So một lần chạy của model A với một lần chạy của model B chẳng nói lên được gì.
  • Data contamination: test set của bạn có thể đã nằm trong data fine-tune, hoặc trong pre-training data của base model nếu bạn lấy từ benchmark công khai.

Cách chữa không cần gì cao siêu: một golden dataset do chính bạn viết, chạy nhiều seed, rồi tính confidence interval thay vì chỉ nhìn một con số trung bình.

Kiến trúc tối thiểu của một eval harness 

flowchart LR
  D[golden.jsonl] --> R[Runner]
  M1[Base model] --> R
  M2[Model mới hoặc LoRA] --> R
  R --> S[Scorers: exact, contains, regex]
  R --> J[LLM judge pairwise]
  S --> A[Bootstrap CI]
  J --> A
  A --> G{CI gate}

Có 3 thành phần chính:

  1. Dataset: file JSONL, mỗi dòng là một test case. Nên có 100–300 case lấy từ use case thật của bạn, như log production đã ẩn danh hay các ticket support. Đừng copy từ MMLU hay GSM8K.
  2. Scorers: ưu tiên chấm bằng code như exact match, contains, regex hay JSON schema validation. Chỉ dùng LLM-as-judge cho các câu trả lời mở.
  3. Aggregation: tính mean kèm bootstrap CI 95%, rồi so với baseline.

File evals/golden.jsonl trông như sau:

{"id": "vn-001", "input": "Thủ đô của Việt Nam là gì? Chỉ trả lời tên.", "expected": "Hà Nội", "scorer": "exact"}
{"id": "fmt-002", "input": "Trả về JSON có key status cho đơn hàng đã giao.", "expected": "\"status\"", "scorer": "contains"}

Code: harness với Python + OpenAI-compatible API

Mình dùng openai>=1.50 và trỏ vào endpoint local: Ollama 0.4+ (/v1) hoặc vLLM 0.6+ đều chạy được, không tốn tiền API.

# eval_harness.py — Python 3.12, openai>=1.50
import json, re, random, statistics, sys
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url='http://localhost:11434/v1', api_key='ollama')

def load(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

def ask(model, prompt, seed, temperature=0.7):
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': prompt}],
        temperature=temperature, seed=seed, max_tokens=256,
    )
    return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

SCORERS = {
    'exact': lambda out, exp: float(out.strip().lower() == exp.strip().lower()),
    'contains': lambda out, exp: float(exp.lower() in out.lower()),
    'regex': lambda out, exp: float(re.search(exp, out) is not None),
}

def bootstrap_ci(scores, n=2000, alpha=0.05):
    means = sorted(
        statistics.mean(random.choices(scores, k=len(scores))) for _ in range(n)
    )
    return means[int(n * alpha / 2)], means[int(n * (1 - alpha / 2)) - 1]

def run(model, dataset, seeds=(1, 2, 3)):
    rows, scores = [], []
    for case in dataset:
        scorer = SCORERS[case['scorer']]
        per_seed = [scorer(ask(model, case['input'], s), case['expected']) for s in seeds]
        score = statistics.mean(per_seed)
        scores.append(score)
        rows.append({'id': case['id'], 'score': score})
    lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(scores)
    return {'model': model, 'mean': statistics.mean(scores), 'ci95': [lo, hi], 'rows': rows}

if __name__ == '__main__':
    random.seed(42)
    model, path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    print(json.dumps(run(model, load(path)), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))

Có hai điểm đáng chú ý. Thứ nhất, mỗi case chạy 3 seed và lấy trung bình, nên một lần "may mắn" không làm lệch kết quả. Thứ hai, bootstrap CI cho bạn biết khoảng dao động thật. Nếu base model đạt 0.72 [0.66, 0.78] và model mới đạt 0.75 [0.69, 0.81], hai khoảng chồng lên nhau gần hết. Bạn chưa có bằng chứng là model mới tốt hơn, dù trung bình cao hơn 3 điểm.

LLM-as-judge: dùng được, nhưng phải chống position bias

Với các câu trả lời mở như tóm tắt hay giải thích code, không có cách nào chấm bằng regex. Lúc đó bạn cần một model mạnh hơn làm giám khảo. Có điều judge model nổi tiếng là thiên vị vị trí: nó hay chọn câu trả lời đứng đầu tiên. Cách xử lý đơn giản nhất là chấm hai lần và đổi chỗ.

sequenceDiagram
  participant H as Harness
  participant J as Judge
  H->>J: Q, A=base, B=new
  J-->>H: B
  H->>J: Q, A=new, B=base
  J-->>H: A
  Note over H: Nhất quán thì new thắng, mâu thuẫn thì tính tie
JUDGE_PROMPT = '''Bạn là giám khảo nghiêm khắc.
Câu hỏi: {q}
Câu trả lời A: {a}
Câu trả lời B: {b}
Câu nào đúng và hữu ích hơn? Chỉ trả lời MỘT ký tự: A, B hoặc T (hòa).'''

def judge_once(q, a, b, judge_model='qwen2.5:32b'):
    out = ask(judge_model, JUDGE_PROMPT.format(q=q, a=a, b=b), seed=0, temperature=0)
    return out[:1].upper()

def pairwise(q, ans_base, ans_new):
    first = judge_once(q, ans_base, ans_new)   # new ở vị trí B
    second = judge_once(q, ans_new, ans_base)  # new ở vị trí A
    if first == 'B' and second == 'A':
        return 'new'
    if first == 'A' and second == 'B':
        return 'base'
    return 'tie'  # judge đổi ý khi đổi chỗ => kết quả không đáng tin

Mẹo thực tế: hãy log lại tỉ lệ tie do mâu thuẫn. Nếu tỉ lệ này vượt khoảng 30%, judge của bạn quá yếu so với task hoặc prompt chấm đang mơ hồ. Lúc đó nên sửa judge trước rồi mới tin vào kết quả. Ngoài ra, đừng bao giờ để một model tự chấm chính nó, vì self-preference bias là có thật.

Gắn vào CI: không có bằng chứng thì không merge

Phần cuối là biến eval thành một gate. Script bash dưới đây chạy được trong GitHub Actions hoặc GitLab CI nếu runner có GPU, hoặc gọi sang một inference server nội bộ.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# eval_gate.sh — cần jq 1.7+, bc
set -euo pipefail

python eval_harness.py qwen2.5:7b      evals/golden.jsonl > base.json
python eval_harness.py my-lora:latest  evals/golden.jsonl > new.json

echo "base: $(jq .mean base.json) $(jq -c .ci95 base.json)"
echo "new : $(jq .mean new.json) $(jq -c .ci95 new.json)"

# Liệt kê các case bị regress để review bằng mắt
jq -r --slurpfile b base.json '
  .rows[] as $r
  | ($b[0].rows[] | select(.id == $r.id) | .score) as $s
  | select($r.score < $s)
  | "REGRESS \($r.id): \($s) -> \($r.score)"' new.json

NEW_LO=$(jq '.ci95[0]' new.json)
BASE_HI=$(jq '.ci95[1]' base.json)

if (( $(echo "$NEW_LO > $BASE_HI" | bc -l) )); then
  echo "✅ Cải thiện rõ ràng, CI không chồng nhau"
else
  echo "⚠️  Chưa đủ bằng chứng — đừng claim là tốt hơn"
  exit 1
fi

Điều kiện "CI không chồng nhau" khá bảo thủ, nhưng mình thấy nó an toàn. Muốn chặt chẽ hơn thì bạn có thể chuyển sang paired bootstrap trên hiệu số từng case. Có một điều quan trọng không kém: danh sách REGRESS. Ngay cả khi điểm trung bình tăng, model mới vẫn có thể làm hỏng đúng những case quan trọng nhất của bạn.

Kết luận

Những tranh cãi kiểu "model X được cải thiện" trên HN sẽ còn lặp lại, và bạn không cần phải là nạn nhân, dù ở vai người viết hay người đọc. Các bước nên làm ngay:

  1. Viết golden set 100 case từ use case thật trong tuần này. Đây là tài sản quý nhất, quý hơn cả code harness.
  2. Chạy nhiều seed và báo cáo kèm CI 95%. Không có CI thì con số trung bình gần như vô nghĩa.
  3. Ưu tiên scorer bằng code. Chỉ dùng LLM-as-judge cho câu trả lời mở, luôn đổi chỗ A/B, và theo dõi tỉ lệ judge mâu thuẫn.
  4. Gắn eval vào CI cho mọi thay đổi về prompt, LoRA hay model version, và review danh sách regress trước khi merge.
  5. Version hóa dataset cùng code, và đừng bao giờ đưa nó vào data fine-tune.

Khi đọc một claim kiểu "model tốt hơn X%", hãy hỏi ngay ba câu: test trên bao nhiêu case, có baseline không, và confidence interval là bao nhiêu. Nếu không ai trả lời được, đó mới chỉ là cảm giác chứ chưa phải kết quả.

title: One 4k prompt costs a serving node as much as 900 generated tokens
description:
A node serving Llama-3.1-70B, 32 conversations streaming, GPU pegged at 95%. Then someone pastes a document. Every live conversation freezes for most of a second, then resumes. Nothing is broken and no config is wrong. The prefill is doing exactly what the arithmetic says it should, and the arithmetic says it costs far more than the time-to-first-token graphs imply.

Time to first token measures the request that just arrived. It does not measure the tax that request levies on the requests already in flight. That tax has a number, and it is bigger than most capacity plans assume.

What one decode step costs

Take the published config.json for Llama-3.1-70B: 80 layers, 8192 hidden, 64 heads, 8 KV heads of 128. FP8 weights are 70.5 GB. FP8 KV cache is 160 KiB per token.

A decode step reads every weight plus the cache of every sequence in the batch. On one H100 SXM at 3.35 TB/s, that sets a floor:

Batch @ 4k ctx Step time Reads Per-sequence
1 21.3 ms 71 GB 47.0 tok/s
8 22.7 76 GB 44.2
32 27.5 92 GB 36.4
64 33.9 114 GB 29.5
256 72.3 242 GB 13.8
512 123.6 414 GB 8.1

Read it as aggregate bandwidth, since 70 B FP8 does not fit on one card: at batch 64 the table says a node sustains 1,889 tokens per second. Published 70B FP8 node benchmarks sit in that band, which is my check that the rest of this arithmetic is not invented. Every sequence in the batch gets its next token from the same weight read, which is why per-sequence speed falls only 6% when the batch grows eightfold: 47.0 to 44.2 tok/s, for eight times the users.

At 4k context this step never becomes compute-bound: each sequence adds 671 MB of cache read, which costs 0.20 ms of bandwidth against 0.18 ms of FLOPs, so memory stays the binding constraint at every batch in the table. At 512-token context the crossing lands near batch 137, and past it the batch stops being free.

What one prefill costs

Prefill is the opposite workload: compute-bound, quadratic in context.

FLOPs per prompt are 2 × N × T for the linear work plus 4 × L × H × d_head × T² for attention. At 70.5B parameters, 40% MFU, and 1,979 TFLOP/s of FP8 peak on an H100:

Context Linear TFLOP Attention TFLOP Attention share Time @ 40% MFU
1,024 144 3 2% 186 ms
4,096 578 44 7% 786 ms
16,384 2,312 704 23% 3,809 ms
32,768 4,624 2,815 38% 9,397 ms

A 4k prompt is 786 ms of one node's compute. At 30% MFU it is 1,048 ms; at 60% it is 524 ms. The band matters for the constant, not for the ordering.

Notice what is not in that budget: the KV write. A 4k prompt at FP8 writes 671 MB, which is 0.2 ms of bandwidth. Prefill is not a cache problem. It is FLOPs, and on a node that is already serving decode, it is FLOPs that arrive on top of a workload with no spare time.

The conversion nobody does

At batch 32, one generated token across the whole batch is 27.5 ms ÷ 32 = 0.86 ms of GPU time. A 4k prefill is 786 ms. Divide.

One 4k prompt costs the GPU time of 914 generated tokens.

That is the sentence I would put on the capacity spreadsheet. It is also not, by itself, the user-visible cost. The user-visible cost is that the prefill does not run on spare capacity. It runs instead of the decode step, and every live stream waits. Thirty-two sequences each lose 786 ms of wall clock, which at 36 tok/s is roughly 29 tokens each, or about 915 tokens of aggregate progress. The two numbers agree because they are the same number.

So a batch that looks efficient by tokens per second is exactly the batch that makes one arriving document expensive. Bigger batch, more user-seconds per prefill, same 786 ms of GPU.

Chunked prefill does not refund it

The standard fix is to split the prefill into chunks and interleave them with decode. It is a real fix for the spike and it is not a fix for the cost.

The break-even chunk is the chunk that takes exactly as long as one decode step. At 70 B FP8 that works out to 119 tokens, and it is independent of batch size: the decode step is memory-bound, so its time does not move with batch, while a prefill chunk is compute-bound with fixed coefficients.

Chunk Chunk time Decode steps lost
128 23 ms 1.08
512 92 ms 4.33
1,024 186 ms 8.75

A 512-token chunk is 4.3 decode steps, repeated eight times for a 4k prompt. Total stall: unchanged. Maximum stall: divided by eight. vLLM's 512 default is a compromise between a number this table can name and a cost this table cannot: tiny chunks raise kernel-launch overhead and shrink the GEMMs, so prefill throughput falls. I do not have a measurement for that penalty, so I will not put a number on it.

If you care about inter-token latency, the target is a chunk near 119 tokens. At 20 tok/s the normal gap between tokens is 50 ms; a 512-token chunk inserts 92 ms, about two tokens' worth of silence, every 512 prompt tokens. A 128-token chunk inserts 23 ms, which is invisible, and probably costs you prefill throughput. That trade is where the tuning lives.

Long context makes it worse in a way chunking cannot reach

Look at the attention column again. At 4k, attention is 7% of the prefill. At 32k it is 38%, and the term is quadratic in T, so it is untouched by chunk size: splitting a 32k prompt into 64 chunks still does 2,815 TFLOP of attention work, now with worse arithmetic intensity. Chunking converts a spike into a plateau. It does not move the plateau, and at long context the plateau is where the time went.

This is the same curve that makes long-context decode expensive, arriving from the other side.

The capacity number for a mixed workload

Put the two together. A node has one GPU-second per second. A 4k prefill consumes 0.79 of them. Decode at batch 32 consumes 0.86 ms per generated token.

Prefills/s (4k) GPU spent on prefill Decode sequences that still fit Per-sequence
0.25 20% 25.7 36.4 tok/s
0.50 39% 19.4 36.4
1.00 79% 6.9 36.4
2.00 100% 0 —

One document per second eats four-fifths of the node. Two per second and the decode queue never drains; throughput does not fall, it stops. If you have ever wondered why a chat product's p99 collapses in the late afternoon while utilization reads healthy, this table is the shape of the answer.

Why prefill/decode disaggregation became practical

If the interference is structural, the clean answer is separate pools and ship the cache. The cost is the transfer, and it is now small.

Link 671 MB KV for a 4k prompt
NVLink 900 GB/s 0.7 ms
400G InfiniBand 13.4 ms
100G InfiniBand 53.7 ms

Against a 786 ms prefill, 400G adds 1.7%. On 100G it adds 7% and, worse, a variable 7%. That is roughly the story of why the architecture was proposed years ago and deployed later: the compute math was always fine, the interconnect was not.

The script

Everything above, runnable. Change MFU and the conclusions scale; change the config and the ordering does not.

L, D, H, KVH, HD = 80, 8192, 64, 8, 128   # Llama-3.1-70B config.json
N, BW, FPEAK = 70.55e9, 3.35e12, 1979e12  # params; H100 SXM bytes/s; FP8 TFLOP/s
KV = 2 * L * KVH * HD                     # bytes per token, FP8

def step(b, mfu=0.4, ctx=4096):
    mem = (N + b * KV * ctx) / BW
    flop = 2 * N * b / (mfu * FPEAK)
    return max(mem, flop)

def prefill(T, mfu=0.4):
    return (2 * N * T + 4 * L * H * HD * T * T) / (mfu * FPEAK)

s32 = step(32)
print(f"one 4k prefill = {prefill(4096)/s32*32:.0f} generated tokens")
print(f"break-even chunk = {step(1)*0.4*FPEAK/(2*N):.0f} tokens")
print(f"chunk 512 = {prefill(512)/step(1):.2f} decode steps")

If you run it and disagree with a constant, that is the useful kind of disagreement: the MFU and the peak are the two numbers I chose rather than derived, and both are checkable on your own card.

What I would measure next

The one thing this arithmetic cannot tell you is how much prefill throughput the 119-token chunk costs. That needs a card, a profiler, and two configs. If you have run that sweep, I would like the numbers; the comment section is where I keep the corrections.

The rest of this series, including the decode and KV-cache pieces these constants come from, is in my archive and on my dev.to profile.

Assumptions: FP8 weights and cache, no tensor parallelism overhead, no continuous-batching scheduler loss, 40% MFU for both prefill and decode. Every table is arithmetic from the published config and the H100 datasheet, not a benchmark.

title: GPT-5.6 Sol vs Claude Opus 4.8 for Coding: A Reproducible CSV-to-JSON Importer Test
description:
This article was written with AI assistance. On November 3, 2026 I ran GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 against the same CSV-to-JSON importer task via the Crazyrouter API and I describe exactly what the generated code did on my machine. I did not add polish numbers or production uptime claims that I did not measure.

The scenario I kept in mind is the one most of us actually meet: a weekly export from a spreadsheet, a validation step, and a downstream service that only wants a well-formed JSON array. The pipeline is small, but every stage has a sharp edge: a wrong price cast, a header you did not expect, or an output path pointing at the source. If an AI is going to help, I want its code to survive those edges, not to look clever on the happy path.

Why I framed GPT-5.6 Sol vs Claude Opus 4.8 around a reusable local tool

Benchmarks measure a model against a battery of problems. A pipeline measures a tool against the problems that recur on your machine, every week. Those are different jobs. Asking GPT-5.6 Sol or Claude Opus 4.8 to write me a standalone Node.js program means I can version-control it, add it to CI as a dry run, and get a predictable exit code — none of which I get from pasting a CSV into a chat window each Monday.

The spec I gave both models was identical: produce import-products.cjs with no third-party dependencies. Accept a UTF-8 CSV (BOM allowed), handle CRLF/LF, quoted commas, and in-quote newlines. Accept any order of the header aliases sku|SKU|Product ID, name|Product Name, price|Price, stock|Stock. Reject missing, duplicated, or unknown columns. Enforce two-decimal prices converted to integer cents and non-negative integer stock. Only on full validation success, write the JSON array via a temp file + rename.

The sharpest clause was the failure contract: if the CSV is malformed, if any row violates the rules, or if the input and output arguments resolve to the same file, log to stderr and exit non-zero without touching the input or any pre-existing output. That last condition is the one both models' first drafts quietly ignored.

The prompt I gave GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8

I used a Simplified Chinese prompt (that is my working language for this project) and sent two rounds through Crazyrouter's OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1/chat/completions, with the model IDs gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-4-8. Round one was the spec above. Round two fed each model exactly one piece of information: "When input and output pointed at the same file, your first version overwrote the source CSV. Add real file-identity checks and refuse to run in that case. Keep everything else."

POST /v1/chat/completions HTTP/1.1
Host: api.crazyrouter.com
Authorization: Bearer <key read in-process from a local file>
Content-Type: application/json

{"model":"gpt-5.6-sol","messages":[...],"temperature":0}

Round-two outputs for both models added an fs.realpathSync + inode comparison (or the equivalent on Windows) and now bail out on the collision. No manual edits were applied to the generated code; whatever shipped from the API is what I ran.

Running the GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 scripts safely

I treat an AI-authored script the way I treat any dependency change: pin the inputs, run against fixtures, and watch the exit code. The simplest CI step is literally two lines:

node import-products.cjs tests/good.csv build/products.json
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "import blocked"; exit 1; fi

With both revised scripts in place, 23 local input scenarios all behaved as expected: happy paths produced the correct JSON; malformed rows aborted with stderr output and left the previous products.json untouched; shuffled headers in Simplified Chinese and English both mapped correctly; the "same path for input and output" case now refuses to run.

Two concrete fixtures worth stealing:

  • Alias-shuffled header, with a quoted comma field. Confirms the alias table and the CSV parser cooperate. 
  Stock, Product Name ,Product ID,Price
  7,"Mug, Blue",A01,12.30
  • Deliberately bad price. Confirms the failure path leaves the old JSON alone. I used 12.3 (only one decimal). Both revised scripts aborted; the pre-existing products.json was byte-identical before and after.

Downstream code should always key off the exit code, not off the presence of the file. "The file still exists" is not the same as "today's import succeeded." That is the single most important discipline when AI-generated scripts enter a pipeline.

Where GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 diverged

Treat the following as observations on this specific task, not as a verdict on either model.

Isolated parser sampling. I asked each model, three times, with no revision round, to produce just the parseCsv(input) helper for a tricky input with an unclosed quote and a multi-line comment field. All three GPT-5.6 Sol samples parsed the records correctly. Of the three Claude Opus 4.8 samples, one was correct; the other two emitted empty rows or crashed. If your job is to drop a single parsing helper into an existing codebase and move on, this one small-N sample points toward GPT-5.6 Sol for the sliver of work. It is not a statement about long-form coding ability.

Error messages. With a malformed price, Claude Opus 4.8's revised script printed a human-readable explanation in Simplified Chinese ("the price must have exactly two decimals, e.g. 12.30"). GPT-5.6 Sol's revised script printed an English message that included the offending logical record number. For long CSVs, the record number is the fastest way to find the problem line in your editor; for short files, the explanation is friendlier.

Lenient price acceptance. I fed 01.00 as a price. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected it (leading-zero outside the two-decimal rule). Claude Opus 4.8 accepted it and emitted 100 cents. Neither math is wrong; the spec simply did not say whether a leading zero in the integer part was acceptable. That is a reminder to pin the rule yourself before you blame a model: the "right" answer depends on your accounting conventions.

Picking between GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 for your pipeline

For the complete CLI tool, both models shipped a working, safety-checked version after one targeted revision. If you already have a preferred provider, keep it and spend the saved time on the business rules: Should A01 and A01 be the same SKU? Should a missing stock cell default to zero or abort? Should a leading-zero price be accepted or refused? These are decisions a model cannot make for you, and they are what will actually break production.

For a surgical, single-function drop-in, GPT-5.6 Sol was more consistent on this parser sample. For an interactive debugging experience with human-readable error messages (and if you can live with the Simplified Chinese locale), Claude Opus 4.8's revised output was pleasant to read. Both are valid defaults; neither is a universal "better coder."

If you want to replicate this, start from Crazyrouter's coding model catalog and the quickstart linked above. Pin your temperature, pin your prompt, write your failure contract before you write the happy path, and keep the fixtures that break the first version — they are the ones that will keep the next version honest.

All runs on November 3, 2026, Node.js v24.21.0, exactly one revision round per model. No new paid calls were made for this write-up beyond the two rounds described; the 23 scenarios are repeated local invocations of the same generated tool, not independent model challenges.

title: Convert Word (DOCX) to Markdown With Python (Standard Library Only) for LLM Prompts and Chatbot Knowledge
description:
A lot of company knowledge still lives in Word files: refund policies, onboarding guides, SOPs, proposal templates. If you want that content in a prompt, a RAG index or a chatbot's knowledge base, Markdown is a better format than the .docx itself or a flat text dump. It keeps headings, lists, tables and links, and it is easy to diff, chunk and review.

This post builds a DOCX-to-Markdown converter with Python's standard library only (zipfile and xml.etree.ElementTree), so it runs in a CI job, a small container or a serverless function without a pip install. It handles headings, bold and italic, links, nested bullet and numbered lists, tables, line breaks, images and tracked changes.

Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this post. Appie has a free DOCX to Markdown converter and a few other Word tools, mentioned near the end. The script below does not depend on them.

Earlier posts in this series cover converting CSV and JSON to Markdown tables and converting PDFs to Markdown for RAG.

What is inside a .docx

A .docx file is a ZIP archive of XML files. Rename one to .zip and open it, and you will find:

  • word/document.xml: the body. Paragraphs are <w:p>, runs of text with the same formatting are <w:r>, the text itself is in <w:t>, tables are <w:tbl>.
  • word/styles.xml: style definitions. A paragraph only says <w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/>; this file tells you what that style is.
  • word/numbering.xml: list definitions. A list item only says "numbering 3, level 1"; this file tells you whether that level is a bullet or a number.
  • word/_rels/document.xml.rels: where hyperlinks point and which file in word/media/ each image is.

So a converter has four jobs: read the body in order, look up styles to find headings, look up numbering to tell bullets from numbers, and resolve relationships for links and images.

What a useful converter has to do

  1. Find headings by style name, not style ID. IDs such as Heading1 can differ between Word languages and between editors. The name (heading 1) and the outline level are more reliable.
  2. Merge runs. Word splits text into runs for reasons you cannot see (spell check, edits, language tags). Without merging, you get output like **annual** **plans**.
  3. Handle "off" switches. <w:b w:val="0"/> means not bold. A naive check for the <w:b> tag gets this wrong.
  4. Handle both kinds of lists: numbering set directly on the paragraph, and numbering that comes from a style such as "List Bullet 2".
  5. Keep tables as tables, with pipes escaped and multi-paragraph cells joined.
  6. Keep tracked insertions and skip tracked deletions, so you convert the text a reader sees.
  7. Not pass through dangerous links. A Word file can contain javascript: link targets.

The script

Save this as docx2md.py. It was tested with Python 3.13.5 on the files described below.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Convert a .docx file to Markdown with the Python standard library only."""
import posixpath
import re
import sys
import zipfile
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from pathlib import Path

W = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main}"
R = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships}"
A = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/main}"
WP = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing}"
PR = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships}"


def read_xml(z, name):
    try:
        return ET.fromstring(z.read(name))
    except KeyError:
        return None


def is_on(el):
    """<w:b/> means on; <w:b w:val="0"/> or "false" means off."""
    return el is not None and el.get(W + "val", "true") not in ("0", "false", "none")


class Docx:
    def __init__(self, path, media_dir=None):
        self.z = zipfile.ZipFile(path)
        self.media_dir = Path(media_dir) if media_dir else None
        self.heading_level = self._load_styles()
        self.num_formats = self._load_numbering()
        self.rels = self._load_rels()
        self.counters = {}

    def _load_styles(self):
        """Map styleId -> heading level, using the style name or outline level."""
        levels, self.style_num, self.style_depth = {}, {}, {}
        root = read_xml(self.z, "word/styles.xml")
        if root is None:
            return levels
        for st in root.iter(W + "style"):
            sid = st.get(W + "styleId")
            name_el = st.find(W + "name")
            name = (name_el.get(W + "val") if name_el is not None else "").lower()
            m = re.fullmatch(r"heading (\d)", name)
            outline = st.find(f"{W}pPr/{W}outlineLvl")
            deep = re.fullmatch(r"list (?:bullet|number) (\d)", name)  # "List Bullet 2"
            if deep:
                self.style_depth[sid] = int(deep.group(1)) - 1
            num = st.find(f"{W}pPr/{W}numPr")  # list styles such as "List Bullet"
            if num is not None and num.find(W + "numId") is not None:
                ilvl = num.find(W + "ilvl")
                self.style_num[sid] = (num.find(W + "numId").get(W + "val"),
                                       ilvl.get(W + "val") if ilvl is not None else "0")
            if name == "title":
                levels[sid] = 1
            elif m:
                levels[sid] = int(m.group(1))
            elif outline is not None:
                levels[sid] = int(outline.get(W + "val")) + 1
        return levels

    def _load_numbering(self):
        """Map (numId, ilvl) -> numFmt such as 'bullet' or 'decimal'."""
        fmts = {}
        root = read_xml(self.z, "word/numbering.xml")
        if root is None:
            return fmts
        abstract = {}
        for an in root.findall(W + "abstractNum"):
            lv = {}
            for lvl in an.findall(W + "lvl"):
                f = lvl.find(W + "numFmt")
                lv[lvl.get(W + "ilvl")] = f.get(W + "val") if f is not None else "bullet"
            abstract[an.get(W + "abstractNumId")] = lv
        for num in root.findall(W + "num"):
            ref = num.find(W + "abstractNumId").get(W + "val")
            for ilvl, fmt in abstract.get(ref, {}).items():
                fmts[(num.get(W + "numId"), ilvl)] = fmt
        return fmts

    def _load_rels(self):
        rels = {}
        root = read_xml(self.z, "word/_rels/document.xml.rels")
        if root is not None:
            for rel in root.findall(PR + "Relationship"):
                rels[rel.get("Id")] = rel.get("Target")
        return rels

    # ---- inline content -------------------------------------------------
    def runs(self, parent, link=None):
        """Yield (text, bold, italic, link) segments for a paragraph."""
        for child in parent:
            if child.tag == W + "r":
                rpr = child.find(W + "rPr")
                bold = rpr is not None and is_on(rpr.find(W + "b"))
                ital = rpr is not None and is_on(rpr.find(W + "i"))
                for el in child:
                    if el.tag == W + "t":
                        yield el.text or "", bold, ital, link
                    elif el.tag == W + "tab":
                        yield " ", bold, ital, link
                    elif el.tag in (W + "br", W + "cr"):
                        yield "\n", False, False, None
                    elif el.tag == W + "drawing":
                        yield self.image(el), False, False, None
            elif child.tag == W + "hyperlink":
                rid = child.get(R + "id")
                target = self.rels.get(rid) if rid else None
                if target is None and child.get(W + "anchor"):
                    target = "#" + child.get(W + "anchor")
                if target and not re.match(r"(https?:|mailto:|#)", target):
                    target = None  # drop javascript:, file: and other odd targets
                yield from self.runs(child, target)
            elif child.tag in (W + "ins", W + "smartTag", W + "sdt", W + "sdtContent"):
                yield from self.runs(child, link)  # tracked insertions, content controls

    def image(self, drawing):
        blip = drawing.find(f".//{A}blip")
        doc_pr = drawing.find(f".//{WP}docPr")
        alt = (doc_pr.get("descr") or doc_pr.get("name") or "") if doc_pr is not None else ""
        target = self.rels.get(blip.get(R + "embed")) if blip is not None else None
        if not target:
            return ""
        name = posixpath.basename(target)
        if self.media_dir:
            self.media_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            part = posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join("word", target))
            (self.media_dir / name).write_bytes(self.z.read(part))
            return f"![{alt}]({self.media_dir.name}/{name})"  # relative to the .md file
        return f"![{alt}]({name})"

    def inline(self, p):
        # merge neighbouring segments with the same formatting
        merged = []
        for text, b, i, link in self.runs(p):
            if merged and merged[-1][1:] == [b, i, link] and not text.startswith("!["):
                merged[-1][0] += text
            else:
                merged.append([text, b, i, link])
        out = []
        for text, b, i, link in merged:
            core = text.strip()
            if not core:
                out.append(text)
                continue
            lead = text[: len(text) - len(text.lstrip())]
            trail = text[len(text.rstrip()):]
            mark = "**" * b + "*" * i
            core = f"{mark}{core}{mark[::-1]}"
            if link:
                core = f"[{core}]({link})"
            out.append(lead + core + trail)
        return "".join(out)

    # ---- blocks ---------------------------------------------------------
    def paragraph(self, p):
        self.last_num = None
        text = self.inline(p).strip()
        ppr = p.find(W + "pPr")
        style = ppr.find(W + "pStyle") if ppr is not None else None
        sid = style.get(W + "val") if style is not None else None
        num = ppr.find(W + "numPr") if ppr is not None else None
        if not text:
            return None
        if sid in self.heading_level:
            plain = text.replace("**", "").replace("\n", " ")  # headings are bold already
            return "#" * min(self.heading_level[sid], 6) + " " + plain
        num_id, ilvl = self.style_num.get(sid, (None, "0"))
        if num is not None and num.find(W + "numId") is not None:
            num_id = num.find(W + "numId").get(W + "val")
            ilvl_el = num.find(W + "ilvl")
            ilvl = ilvl_el.get(W + "val") if ilvl_el is not None else ilvl
        self.last_num = num_id
        if num_id and num_id != "0":
            fmt = self.num_formats.get((num_id, ilvl), "bullet")
            depth = int(ilvl) + self.style_depth.get(sid, 0)
            # restart deeper levels when a shallower item appears
            for key in [k for k in self.counters if k[0] == num_id and int(k[1]) > depth]:
                del self.counters[key]
            indent = "    " * depth
            if fmt == "bullet":
                return f"{indent}- {text}"
            n = self.counters[(num_id, ilvl)] = self.counters.get((num_id, ilvl), 0) + 1
            return f"{indent}{n}. {text}"
        if sid and sid.lower() in ("code", "sourcecode", "htmlpreformatted"):
            return f"```\n{''.join(t.text or '' for t in p.iter(W + 't'))}\n```"
        return text.replace("\n", "  \n")

    def table(self, tbl):
        rows = []
        for tr in tbl.findall(W + "tr"):
            cells = []
            for tc in tr.findall(W + "tc"):
                parts = [self.inline(p).strip() for p in tc.iter(W + "p")]
                cell = "<br>".join(x for x in parts if x).replace("\n", "<br>")
                cells.append(cell.replace("|", "\\|"))
            rows.append(cells)
        if not rows:
            return None
        width = max(len(r) for r in rows)
        rows = [r + [""] * (width - len(r)) for r in rows]
        lines = ["| " + " | ".join(rows[0]) + " |", "|" + " --- |" * width]
        lines += ["| " + " | ".join(r) + " |" for r in rows[1:]]
        return "\n".join(lines)

    def convert(self):
        body = read_xml(self.z, "word/document.xml").find(W + "body")
        blocks, prev_list, prev_num, prev_nested = [], False, None, False
        for el in body:
            if el.tag == W + "p":
                md = self.paragraph(el)
            elif el.tag == W + "tbl":
                md = self.table(el)
            elif el.tag == W + "sdt":  # content control, e.g. a table of contents
                inner = el.find(W + "sdtContent")
                paras = inner.findall(W + "p") if inner is not None else []
                md = "\n\n".join(filter(None, (self.paragraph(p) for p in paras)))
            else:
                continue
            if not md:
                continue
            if md.startswith("```\n") and blocks and blocks[-1].endswith("\n```"):
                blocks[-1] = blocks[-1][:-3] + md[4:]  # join consecutive code lines
                continue
            is_list = bool(re.match(r"\s*(-|\d+\.) ", md))
            same_list = is_list and prev_list and (md[0] == " " or prev_nested or self.last_num == prev_num)
            sep = "\n" if same_list else "\n\n"
            blocks.append((sep if blocks else "") + md)
            prev_list, prev_num = is_list, (self.last_num if is_list else None)
            prev_nested = is_list and md[0] == " "
        return "".join(blocks).strip() + "\n"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        sys.exit("usage: docx2md.py input.docx [media_dir] > output.md")
    print(Docx(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None).convert(), end="")

Run it:

python3 docx2md.py policy.docx > policy.md          # images referenced by file name
python3 docx2md.py policy.docx media > policy.md    # also extracts images into ./media

How the pieces fit

  • _load_styles maps each style ID to a heading level, using the style name (title, heading 1 to heading 6) or an outline level. It also records list styles such as "List Bullet" that carry their own numbering, and treats "List Bullet 2" or "List Number 3" as one or two levels deeper.
  • _load_numbering resolves each numId and level to a format. Word stores list formats in two hops (num points to abstractNum), which is why there are two loops.
  • runs walks a paragraph and yields (text, bold, italic, link) segments. It follows hyperlinks, tracked insertions (w:ins) and content controls. Deleted text lives in w:delText, which it never reads, so tracked deletions drop out.
  • inline merges neighbouring segments with identical formatting, then puts the ** and * markers inside any leading or trailing spaces, because ** bold** is not valid Markdown emphasis.
  • paragraph decides between heading, list item, code block and plain paragraph. Numbered items keep a counter per list and level, and deeper counters reset when a shallower item appears.
  • convert walks the body in order, so text and tables stay in their original sequence, and puts list items on consecutive lines so they render as one list.

Try it on a test document

We built a small test file with python-docx (used only to create the fixture; the converter does not need it). It has a Title, Heading 1 and Heading 2, a paragraph with a bold run split in two, an italic run, a bold external link and a run with bold explicitly turned off, a numbered list, a bullet list with a "List Bullet 2" item, a table with a pipe in a cell and a two-paragraph cell, a soft line break, and an image with alt text.

python3 docx2md.py sample.docx media > sample.md

Output:

# Refund policy

Last updated in the Word file. This intro has an empty paragraph after it.

# Who can ask for a refund

Customers on **annual plans** can ask within *30 days*. Read the [**full terms**](https://example.com/terms) first. Not bold

## Steps

1. Open Billing
2. Click Request refund
3. Pick a reason

What you need:

- Order ID
- Account email
    - Found in the receipt footer
- Reason

## Plans

| Plan | Window | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly | 7 days | Pro \| Team |
| Annual | 30 days | Prorated<br>Second line in cell |

Line one  
Line two after a soft break

![Refund flow diagram](media/image1.png)

The split bold run came out as one **annual plans**, "Not bold" stayed plain, the nested bullet is indented under its parent, the pipe in "Pro | Team" stayed inside its cell, and the image was written to media/image1.png with its alt text.

We also checked three other inputs:

  • A LibreOffice-made file (HTML converted to DOCX with soffice --headless), which puts numbering on each paragraph instead of on styles. Nested numbered items came out as 1., 2. under 1., and a bullet list that followed the numbered list started a new list instead of joining it.
  • calibre's public demo DOCX, a Word document built to exercise many features. Headings, the multi-level numbered and bulleted lists, external and internal links, inline images and simple tables came through. Its "continued list" section, where Word resumes numbering at 3 after an interrupting paragraph, also came out as 3 and 4. Its word/document.xml is about 138 KB; the Markdown is about 10 KB.
  • Edge cases: a tracked change file (the deleted text was dropped and the inserted text kept), a document with a javascript: link (the link was removed and its text kept, while a mailto: link survived), and consecutive paragraphs in a "Code" style (merged into one fenced block).

Convert a folder of Word files

For a shared drive export, convert everything in one pass and keep the folder structure:

from pathlib import Path
from docx2md import Docx

src, dst = Path("docs"), Path("markdown")
for path in sorted(src.rglob("*.docx")):
    if path.name.startswith("~$"):  # Word lock files
        continue
    out = dst / path.relative_to(src).with_suffix(".md")
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    media = out.parent / (out.stem + "_media")
    out.write_text(Docx(path, media).convert(), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"{path} -> {out}")

Each Markdown file gets its own <name>_media folder, and image links are written relative to the .md file, so the output can be moved as a unit. The ~$ check skips the lock files Word leaves next to open documents.

Known limits (and how to extend it)

  • Footnotes, endnotes and comments are dropped. They live in word/footnotes.xml, word/endnotes.xml and word/comments.xml. To keep footnotes, read w:footnoteReference in runs, emit [^n], and append the footnote text at the end.
  • Merged and nested table cells are flattened. Markdown tables cannot express gridSpan, vMerge or a table inside a cell. On calibre's demo, a nested table was folded into a single cell, and a calendar built from merged cells came out with empty columns. Keep such tables as HTML or rebuild them by hand.
  • Formatting from character styles is ignored. Only direct bold and italic are read. Text that is bold because of a style such as "Strong" comes out plain. Add those style IDs to the bold check if your documents rely on them.
  • Text boxes, shapes, headers, footers and drop caps are skipped or come out oddly. A drop cap shows up as a one-letter paragraph.
  • Markdown characters in the text are not escaped. A paragraph that starts with # or 1. will be read as a heading or list by a Markdown renderer. This rarely matters for prompts but matters for published docs.
  • Table of contents entries come through as links with page numbers attached (for example [Tables 3](#_Toc...)). Drop paragraphs whose style name starts with "toc" if you do not want them.
  • Old .doc files are a different binary format. Convert them to .docx first, for example with soffice --headless --convert-to docx file.doc.
  • Untrusted uploads: the script reads files only inside the ZIP and writes images using the base name only, but it does not limit file sizes. If users upload documents, check the uncompressed sizes in zipfile.ZipFile.infolist() before converting and run it with a timeout.

Why not mammoth or pandoc?

Both are mature and handle more of the edge cases above. mammoth is built to produce clean HTML from Word files; its own documentation says its Markdown output is deprecated and recommends converting to HTML and then to Markdown (checked 2 Nov 2026). If you can install dependencies, that route (mammoth, then an HTML-to-Markdown step) or pandoc -f docx -t gfm is a sound choice. The standard-library script makes sense when you cannot add dependencies, want to read and change every rule, or only need the structure that matters for LLM input.

Is Markdown the right target for chatbot knowledge?

Usually yes. Headings give chunkers natural split points, lists and tables keep their shape, and the file is small and easy to review before it goes live. Two habits help: split on ## headings and keep the source document name with each chunk so answers can cite it, and read the converted file once before you index it. A converter cannot tell you that the refund policy in a 2023 Word file is out of date.

When you do not want to run a script

Appie has free browser tools for Word files. Each run asks for a Cloudflare Turnstile check:

  • Convert DOCX to Markdown: upload a .docx; the page says heading styles become Markdown headings and Word tables become Markdown tables. For older .doc files it says to save as .docx first.
  • AI Chat with Your Word Document: upload a .docx and ask what it says. The page says answers have to come from the text you provided, and that headings and tables are included.
  • DOCX to FAQ Generator: writes a Markdown FAQ from a Word file, and the page says it is instructed to skip questions the file cannot answer.

If the end goal is a website chatbot, Appie's AI Chatbots app takes DOCX, PDF, CSV and text uploads as knowledge directly, so you may not need the conversion step at all. If you work from Claude Code or Cursor, Appie's MCP server can add text content to a chatbot (its add_chatbot_content tool takes text, URLs, sitemaps or Content Writer articles, not files), which is where the Markdown from this script fits.

Honest limits of Appie's Word tools

  • One file per run, with a fresh captcha each time. There is no batch mode on the tool pages, so a folder of 200 SOPs is a job for the script.
  • No options are described for footnotes, comments or merged cells, so test a representative file before relying on the output.

FAQ

Does this work with Google Docs exports?
It should, since Google Docs can download a doc as .docx (File > Download > Microsoft Word (.docx)), but we did not test a Google Docs export for this post. Convert one file and check the headings and lists before running a whole folder.

Why are my headings coming out as plain paragraphs?
The author probably made text big and bold instead of applying a Heading style. The script only sees styles. Apply Heading styles in Word, or add a rule that treats short, fully bold paragraphs as headings.

Can I keep underline, strikethrough or colours?
Markdown has no underline or colour. Strikethrough (~~text~~) is supported by GitHub-flavored Markdown; read w:strike in runs the same way as w:b.

How do I split the output for a RAG index?
Split on lines starting with ##, keep the # title with each chunk, and store the source file path as metadata.

Is it safe to run on files from customers?
Treat them as untrusted input: limit sizes, run with a timeout, and review the Markdown before it reaches a public chatbot. The script drops javascript: and file: links, but that is not a full sanitiser.

If you want a website chatbot trained on your documents, you can try Appie's AI Chatbots on the Free plan (500 credits, no credit card) at appie.run.

RG, Founder, Appie.run
