title: Why 80% on OSWorld Required VM Snapshot Rollbacks
description:
If you have ever watched an autonomous computer-use agent work through a desktop operating system, you know the exact moment the rollout dies.

The agent handles the first eight steps cleanly. It launches the browser, navigates to the admin panel, and exports a CSV report. Then, on step nine, it misclicks a dropdown menu, clicks the desktop background to recover, and accidentally dismisses the modal.

From that single mistake, the environment state is corrupted. On step ten, the file the agent expects to inspect does not exist. On step eleven, the agent begins rationalizing why the window looks different. By step fifteen, it is typing random terminal commands into an unfocused window, burning tokens on a trajectory that was doomed five minutes ago.

Every engineering team training computer-use models runs straight into this wall. The standard reaction is to treat the environment like a disposable container: throw the entire virtual machine away, spin up a fresh image, and start the rollout over from step one.

A paper from researchers at MMLab CUHK, Tsinghua University, HKUST(GZ), and JD Explore Academy, titled CUA-Master, takes a different path. Their 27-billion-parameter model, CUA-Master-27B, achieved a score of 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, alongside 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0 and 43.9 on WeaveBench.

The performance did not come from an enormous model or thousands of hours of synthetic self-play. It came from treating operating system interaction like a transactional runtime with snapshot rollbacks.

The cost of throwing away the sandbox

To train a policy that can navigate desktop applications, you need tens of thousands of verified execution trajectories. But real operating systems are stateful and unforgiving.

When a multi-step rollout fails, discarding the entire run creates two problems.

First, it destroys valid compute. If an agent executes thirteen correct actions and stumbles on the fourteenth, tossing the run discards thirteen high-quality demonstration steps. The infrastructure has to reboot the VM, reinstall dependencies, restore seed data, and wait for the model to reproduce the identical prefix.

Second, the alternative is worse. If you do not discard the run and instead let the model attempt recovery, the model frequently generates noisy, self-contradicting actions. If those corrupted suffixes enter your training dataset, the policy learns to hallucinate around broken state instead of executing clean workflows.

CUA-Master solves this with a mechanism called Resilient Trajectory Collection.

Snapshot rollback as a branching search

Instead of restarting from scratch when a task fails or shows operational inefficiency, the CUA-Master runtime uses incremental virtual machine snapshots.

As the agent works, the environment infrastructure creates lightweight snapshots at stable operational boundaries. Each snapshot records the full memory state of the virtual machine alongside a structured signature: active window handles, layout geometry, open file descriptors, and controller metadata.

When the environment verifier flags a failure, a dedicated detector examines three artifacts together: the verifier residuals, the executed trajectory, and the final environment state.

From that comparison, the detector calculates the earliest step where the agent diverged from the intended task state. It also produces execution-grounded diagnostic feedback explaining what went wrong, such as an unhandled modal or a missing target directory, without leaking privileged action labels that would cause distribution mismatch during training.

Once the divergence step is identified, the runtime does not reset the VM to the beginning. It rolls the virtual machine back to the latest snapshot taken immediately before that step.

The policy engine keeps the successful prefix, drops the failed suffix, and resumes execution from the restored state, using the diagnostic feedback as a local hint.

The agent branches outward from the point of failure until the verifier confirms success or exhausts a retry budget. When the run finishes, only the cleanest, shortest passing branch is kept for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Every failed or redundant branch is discarded.

This changes data collection from an all-or-nothing lottery into a localized graph search. The training pipeline collects valid, high-efficiency trajectories while reusing the expensive prefixes that already succeeded.

Mining real video tutorials instead of hallucinating tasks

The second bottleneck in computer-use agents is task diversity.

If you prompt an LLM to generate synthetic desktop tasks, it invents toy problems. It asks to rename three text files in a folder or calculate a sum in a spreadsheet. Those synthetic setups lack the friction of real desktop software, which involves nested menus, modal dialogs, sluggish network tabs, and arbitrary OS quirks.

CUA-Master bootstraps its task pool through open-world seeding. The researchers harvested video tutorials from platforms like YouTube and TikTok.

A raw instructional video cannot be used directly as an agent prompt. Tutorials contain conversational intros, sponsored segments, and non-actionable chatter. The CUA-Master pipeline uses multimodal temporal episode discovery to slice tutorials into discrete software tasks.

From each clip, a dual-path reconstruction pipeline pairs semantic transcript analysis with visual keyframe tracking. It reconstructs the sequence of actions that the human demonstrator executed, verifies them against local application state, and extracts atomic action primitives.

Those primitives then feed an autocatalytic propagation pipeline. The system recombines verified primitives into composable, multi-application workflows that come with executable verification scripts. Instead of training on synthetic guesses, the model trains on composable variations of authentic human software use.

Blending terminal commands with GUI clicks

The third structural design in the framework is a unified hybrid action space.

Pure visual computer-use agents try to solve every problem through the graphical interface. If an agent needs to find a string across fifty files, it opens a file manager, clicks into each folder, and opens text editors one by one. That approach burns dozens of visual inference steps, introduces dozens of opportunities for misclicks, and runs orders of magnitude slower than a simple shell command.

CLI-only agents have the opposite problem: they fail the moment an operation requires interacting with proprietary desktop software, visual canvases, or browser authentications that lack an API.

CUA-Master gives the agent access to both direct GUI primitives (mouse clicks, scrolling, keystrokes) and structured CLI execution (shell.exec). If a task involves searching logs, moving directories, or checking process tables, the agent runs shell commands. When the workflow moves into GIMP, LibreOffice, or Chrome, the agent switches to mouse and keyboard controls.

In ablation benchmarks across hybrid tasks, this dual-interface setup delivered substantial performance and latency improvements over GUI-only baselines.

What builders should take from this

The headline number from the paper is 80.2 on OSWorld Verified for a 27B model, which puts it within striking distance of proprietary frontier models like Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.

The takeaway for engineers building agent systems is about runtime architecture.

If you want reliable agents in complex environments, you cannot treat execution as an uninterrupted straight line. Long-horizon automation requires the harness to manage state boundaries. When an agent inevitably missteps in an OS sandbox, rolling back to a clean checkpoint and retrying the divergence step is far cheaper than rebooting the world or hoping the model talks its way out of trouble.

title: The Two Cybersecurity Problems AI Leaders Need to Understand
description:
By Neil Lawrence @ Trent (Agentic AI Security)

AI is changing cybersecurity in two fundamentally different ways. The first is already familiar: AI makes it faster and easier to find and exploit weaknesses in software. The second is less familiar and potentially more difficult to manage: an AI agent can itself become the source of unexpected and unsafe behavior.

I think of these as Type 1 and Type 2 cybersecurity problems.

The distinction matters because they require different responses. Type 1 calls for stronger versions of the security practices we already know. Type 2 requires us to rethink how authority is delegated to AI systems in the first place.

For business and security leaders, treating both as ordinary software vulnerabilities is a category error. A system can be free of known technical vulnerabilities and still be dangerous if it is able to interpret instructions, choose tools, access data, and take consequential actions in ways its operators did not anticipate.

Type 1: AI Accelerates a Familiar Cybersecurity Problem

A Type 1 cybersecurity problem begins with a vulnerability in conventional software. The vulnerability may be a coding flaw, a misconfiguration, an exposed service, a weak permission, or another defect that an attacker can exploit. There is nothing fundamentally new about this threat. Security teams have dealt with software vulnerabilities for decades. What AI changes is the speed and scale of the process.

An AI system can analyze code, probe applications, identify weak points, and help construct an exploit much faster than a human working alone. Once it finds the vulnerability, it may also be able to exploit it. The underlying weakness is still in the software; AI simply gives the attacker a more capable tool for discovering and using it. This acceleration has serious consequences. State actors and cybercriminals will not voluntarily limit their use of powerful models. If AI reduces the cost of reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, and attack development, defenders must assume those capabilities will be used.

The appropriate response is therefore to improve the speed and reach of defense. Organizations need better visibility into their systems, faster analysis of vulnerabilities, clearer prioritization, and a more efficient path from finding a problem to fixing it. Type 1 is an arms race, but it is an arms race on familiar ground.

Type 2: The AI Agent Becomes the Security Problem

A Type 2 cybersecurity problem is different. It arises when an AI agent acts outside the behavior its operator expected or intended. The difficulty is that instructions given to an agent are not verifiable in the same way as conventional code. A traditional program follows an explicit sequence of operations. An AI agent interprets an objective, reasons about possible actions, selects tools, and adapts its behavior as conditions change. The more capable the agent becomes, the more ways it may find to pursue the goal. That adaptability is often described as intelligence. In deployment, however, it can become a security risk.

Imagine asking an intern to complete a simple research task. To produce a better answer, the intern breaks into a government network and retrieves confidential information. The result may be accurate, and the method may even demonstrate technical skill, but no reasonable manager would say the intern had performed the task appropriately. The intern did not merely make an error. They exceeded the authority they had been given.

The same principle applies to AI agents. If a model is asked to perform well on a hacking challenge, cheating on the challenge or compromising a system outside the test environment may improve its score. That does not make the behavior acceptable. It reveals a form of social stupidity: the system optimized the stated objective while ignoring the boundaries a reasonable person would understand. This is the essence of a Type 2 problem. The threat is not just that an agent encounters a vulnerability. The threat is that the agent itself takes an action that falls outside its intended role.

Type 1 and Type 2 Risks Can Combine

The two categories are conceptually distinct, but they are not isolated from one another. An AI agent may identify a traditional software vulnerability, a Type 1 problem, and then decide to exploit it outside the authority it was given, a Type 2 problem. The vulnerability enables the action, but the agent's decision to cross the boundary creates the second risk.

This combination makes autonomous agents particularly challenging for security teams. The attack surface is no longer limited to code, infrastructure, identities, and configuration. It also includes:

  • The instructions given to the agent
  • The tools and data made available to it
  • The way it interprets its objective
  • The actions it is permitted to take
  • The conditions under which it must stop or escalate
  • The organization's ability to observe and audit its decisions

Security teams therefore need to ask more than, "Is the application vulnerable?" They must also ask, "What authority has been delegated to this system, and how do we know it will remain within that authority?"

Security Now Has Two Fronts

Type 1 cybersecurity problems are familiar weaknesses exploited with greater speed and scale. Type 2 cybersecurity problems emerge when AI agents themselves behave beyond expected boundaries. Organizations must prepare for both.

They need AI-augmented defenses capable of keeping pace with increasingly capable attackers. At the same time, they need disciplined deployment practices that constrain the AI systems operating inside their own businesses. The central lesson is simple: capability is not deployability.

A powerful model is not automatically a safe agent. Before an organization delegates authority, it must understand the boundaries of the system, restrict what it can access and do, and preserve meaningful human oversight.

The businesses that grasp this distinction will be better equipped not only to defend against AI-enabled attacks, but also to avoid creating a new class of security risk within their own operations.

title: Chrome DevTools MCP para agentes: lo probamos y así maneja diálogos y consola ✅ yoDEV Tested
description:
Chrome DevTools MCP para agentes: lo probamos y así maneja diálogos y consola ✅ yoDEV Tested

Chrome DevTools MCP 1.12 avisa a tu agente de IA cuando la página abre un alert de JavaScript y conserva la consola al cambiar de ruta. Lo probamos con un Chrome real.

https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-devtools-november-2026

✅ yoDEV Tested · 3 de noviembre de 2026

chrome-devtools-mcp 1.12.0 con Chrome for Testing 153 headless en Linux, y el menú de DevTools en Chrome 156 en macOS. Los resultados que reportamos como nuestros salen de esa prueba.

El post "New in DevTools: November 2026" de Google, publicado el 20 de octubre, abre con una sección llamada DevTools for Agents. A pesar del nombre, casi nada es interfaz nueva de DevTools: son cambios en chrome-devtools-mcp, el servidor MCP de código abierto que permite a Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Cursor y otros agentes controlar e inspeccionar un Chrome real. Lo único nuevo dentro de DevTools es una entrada de menú.

¿Qué es Chrome DevTools MCP?

Chrome DevTools MCP es un servidor Model Context Protocol, mantenido por el equipo de Chrome DevTools, que le da a un agente de IA las mismas herramientas que usa un desarrollador front-end a mano: navegar, hacer clic, llenar formularios, leer la consola y el registro de red, tomar snapshots y capturas, grabar trazas de rendimiento y ejecutar Lighthouse. Por dentro usa Puppeteer para controlar el navegador. Tu agente lo lanza en local con npx, y el servidor arranca y controla su propia instancia de Chrome.

En la versión que probamos (1.12.0, publicada en npm el 22 de octubre), el servidor expone 32 herramientas, entre ellas click, fill_form, handle_dialog, list_console_messages, get_css_styles, list_network_requests, performance_start_trace, lighthouse_audit y take_heapsnapshot.

Lo cubrimos por primera vez cuando salió como public preview en 2025: Give your AI eyes: Introducing Chrome DevTools MCP.

¿Qué cambió para los agentes en Chrome 155 y 156?

El blog de Chrome lista seis novedades bajo DevTools for Agents:

  • Manejo de diálogos: los diálogos de JavaScript que se abren durante una acción de entrada se manejan automáticamente.
  • Consola persistente: el historial de mensajes de consola se conserva en las navegaciones dentro del mismo documento.
  • Inspección de CSS: una herramienta nueva, get_css_styles, devuelve los estilos calculados y las reglas que aplican, con paginación.
  • Archivo de configuración y control de rutas: un archivo para los flags del servidor y raíces de sistema de archivos personalizadas.
  • Trazas por partes: las grabaciones de rendimiento grandes se procesan por bloques, con un buffer de traza de 1,2 GB por defecto.
  • Menú de configuración: una entrada Get Chrome DevTools for agents en el menú principal de DevTools.

Chrome 155 y 156 están en el canal estable, no solo en Canary o Beta. El servidor se publica en npm con su propio calendario, así que los cambios del servidor los obtienes actualizando el paquete, no actualizando Chrome.

¿Cómo lo probamos?

Ejecutamos chrome-devtools-mcp@1.12.0 en Linux con Node 22 contra Chrome for Testing 153 en modo headless, usando el SDK oficial de MCP para TypeScript como cliente, el mismo protocolo que habla Claude Code. La página de prueba tenía botones que abren un alert, un confirm y un prompt, y otro que llama a history.pushState. La entrada de menú la revisamos por separado en Chrome 156.0.8078.80 en macOS.

¿Qué pasa cuando la página abre un alert, confirm o prompt de JavaScript?

El servidor detecta el diálogo y le devuelve el control al agente de inmediato, pero no lo acepta ni lo cierra por su cuenta. "Manejado automáticamente" significa eso, y es la decisión correcta.

Cuando nuestro agente hizo clic en el botón del alert, la llamada a click respondió en unos 100 ms con:

The element was clicked and it opened a dialog.
# Open dialog
alert: hola desde la página.
Call handle_dialog to handle it before continuing.

Hasta que el agente responde, cualquier otra acción falla con Error: A dialog is open. El agente llama entonces a handle_dialog con action: "accept" o "dismiss", y puede pasar promptText para responder a un prompt(). En nuestra prueba, aceptar un prompt con el texto "Greg" y rechazar un confirm dejó prompt=Greg y confirm=false en la consola, tal como se esperaba.

Por qué importa: el changelog de la versión 1.7.0 corrigió un bloqueo de 180 segundos cuando se abría un diálogo durante una acción. Antes, un alert() inesperado podía congelar al agente tres minutos. Ahora lo ve en la misma respuesta y decide qué hacer, que es justo lo que quieres cuando el diálogo es un "¿Eliminar esto?".

¿El agente conserva la consola de Chrome al navegar?

Sí en las navegaciones dentro de la página, y sí bajo pedido en las cargas completas.

  • Navegación en el mismo documento (un cambio de #hash o history.pushState, que es como la mayoría de los routers de SPA cambian de página): list_console_messages siguió devolviendo todos los mensajes anteriores. No se perdió nada.
  • Navegación completa a otra URL: la lista por defecto empieza de cero con la página nueva. Con includePreservedMessages: true devuelve los mensajes de las últimas tres navegaciones, con los IDs de mensaje en secuencia. El flag --maxNavigationSaved cambia esa ventana, de 1 a 25.

Para depurar una app en React o Vue, esto significa que un error registrado en la ruta anterior sigue ahí cuando el agente lo va a buscar.

¿Qué devuelve get_css_styles?

Devuelve las reglas CSS que aplican a un elemento, en orden de cascada y con la ubicación en la hoja de estilos. Le pasas el uid del elemento que obtienes con take_snapshot. En nuestra prueba, para un botón con una regla de clase y otra dentro de un media query, devolvió primero el bloque @media (min-width: 100px), luego la regla .btn con index:1 como ubicación, y después la hoja de estilos del navegador con las propiedades sobrescritas marcadas como [overloaded]. Los resultados vienen en páginas de 10 reglas por defecto (pageSize, pageIdx), lo que evita que una hoja de estilos grande llene el contexto del agente.

¿Cómo funciona el nuevo archivo de configuración?

Ahora puedes poner las opciones del servidor en un archivo JSON en lugar de una lista larga de argumentos. El servidor busca, en este orden: un archivo indicado con --config, luego cd4a.config.json en $PLUGIN_DATA cuando corre como plugin de un agente, y luego un archivo global:

macOS y Linux: ~/.config/cd4a/config.json
Windows:       %LOCALAPPDATA%/Google/cd4a/config.json

Usa solo el primero que encuentra (no combina archivos) y los flags de la línea de comandos tienen prioridad sobre el archivo. Los nombres de las opciones van en camelCase.

Probamos el archivo global con:

{
  "headless": true,
  "isolated": true,
  "viewport": "800x600",
  "usageStatistics": false
}

Sin ninguna de esas opciones en la línea de comandos, la página reportó una ventana de 800×600 y un navegador headless, así que el archivo se aplicó. La documentación advierte que ni el archivo ni su carpeta deberían ser editables por el agente; si no, el agente podría reescribir sus propios permisos.

¿Qué errores vas a encontrar al usarlo?

Hay dos cambios de comportamiento que conviene conocer antes de conectarlo a tus scripts.

Todas las herramientas ahora piden un pageId. El enrutamiento por ID de página viene activado por defecto (--pageIdRouting). Nuestra primera ejecución falló en cada llamada con pageId: Invalid input: expected number. Agentes como Claude Code leen el esquema de las herramientas y lo resuelven solos, pero si usas el servidor directamente desde un script, llama primero a list_pages y pasa el ID.

El acceso a archivos se limita a la carpeta temporal si tu cliente no soporta MCP roots. Al arrancar, el servidor avisó que el cliente "did not negotiate the MCP roots capability" y que las herramientas que leen o escriben archivos locales quedan restringidas a la carpeta temporal del sistema. Esto afecta, por ejemplo, a guardar capturas, trazas y heap snapshots en tu proyecto. La solución es permitir carpetas concretas con --filesystemRoot (se puede repetir) o, solo con un cliente local de confianza, --allowUnrestrictedPaths. El blog de Google dice que la CLI separada chrome-devtools activa las rutas sin restricción por defecto; la documentación del servidor MCP indica false como valor por defecto, que es lo que vimos.

¿Puede el agente medir el LCP de tu página?

Sí, con una sola llamada. performance_start_trace con reload: true y autoStop: true recargó nuestra página, se detuvo sola después de unos seis segundos y devolvió el LCP (Largest Contentful Paint: 440 ms, divididos en 7 ms de TTFB y 433 ms de retraso de renderizado), el CLS y una lista de insights que el agente puede explorar en detalle. El procesamiento por bloques ocurre por dentro y no se ve desde fuera: con una página de prueba pequeña no podemos verificar el buffer de 1,2 GB ni el troceado, así que eso es la descripción de Google.

Por defecto, las URLs de las trazas se envían a la API de CrUX de Google para traer datos de usuarios reales. Desactívalo con --no-performance-crux si pruebas URLs internas.

¿Qué hace "Get Chrome DevTools for agents"?

En Chrome 156, la entrada está en el menú de tres puntos de DevTools. Al hacer clic abre el repositorio del proyecto en GitHub. Es un atajo a las instrucciones de instalación, no un instalador dentro de DevTools.

¿Cómo instalar Chrome DevTools MCP en Claude Code, Gemini CLI y VS Code?

Necesitas Node.js en versión LTS actual, npm y Chrome estable o más reciente.

Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp
/plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins

Gemini CLI:

gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp

Copilot en VS Code: ejecuta "Chat: Install Plugin From Source" e ingresa ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp.

Cualquier otro cliente MCP (Cursor, Codex y otros), con el bloque de configuración estándar:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}

Flags útiles para añadir: --isolated para un perfil temporal que se borra al cerrar el navegador, --headless para no abrir ventana, --slim para un conjunto reducido de tres herramientas (navegación, ejecución de scripts y capturas) y --no-usage-statistics para no enviar datos de uso.

Una advertencia del propio proyecto: el servidor expone el contenido de su navegador al cliente MCP. No lo apuntes a sesiones con datos que no compartirías con tu agente, y prefiere --isolated antes que tu perfil de todos los días.

¿Chrome DevTools MCP o Playwright MCP?

Si tu trabajo es depurar y medir una app en Chrome, Chrome DevTools MCP; si necesitas Firefox o WebKit, Playwright MCP. Según su README, Playwright MCP (de Microsoft) soporta Chromium, Firefox y WebKit, trabaja sobre el árbol de accesibilidad y también tiene herramientas para diálogos (browser_handle_dialog) y consola (browser_console_messages); las trazas son opcionales con --caps=devtools y no menciona Lighthouse ni análisis de rendimiento. Chrome DevTools MCP solo soporta oficialmente Google Chrome y Chrome for Testing, pero trae lo que viene de DevTools: insights de rendimiento con LCP, lighthouse_audit, heap snapshots y ahora get_css_styles. Playwright MCP no lo probamos para esta nota.

¿Vale la pena actualizarlo?

Sí. Los cambios en diálogos y consola resuelven dos situaciones reales en las que un agente se quedaba trabado o ciego al probar una app web, y ambos se comportaron como describe Google en nuestra prueba. El archivo de configuración hace que el setup sea reproducible en todo el equipo. Solo ten en cuenta el pageId obligatorio y la restricción a la carpeta temporal antes de integrarlo en tus scripts.

Al momento de publicar esta nota, el número de herramientas (32), los valores por defecto y el comportamiento del menú corresponden a la versión 1.12.0 y a Chrome 156; el proyecto publica versiones con frecuencia, así que revisa el changelog antes de depender de un valor por defecto concreto.

¿Y tú? ¿Qué es lo primero que le pedirías revisar a tu agente en el navegador: un error de consola, una petición de red o el rendimiento?

Relacionado: BrowserSkill: cómo darle a Claude Code tu navegador real con la sesión ya iniciada

title: What If We Kept an Agent's Logic with Its Definition?
description:
Exploring programmable agent objects, semantic self-containment, and a single-file approach inspired by Vue.

An application-specific agent can start with a fairly compact definition: a prompt describes its task, and a tool list identifies the operations it can use. At that stage, reviewing the definition can give us a useful picture of the agent.

As the application develops, the role may acquire more specific requirements. It might need to track a budget, react to execution results, preserve progress across restarts, or validate the decision it returns to the application. Those requirements bring programmatic logic into the picture alongside the model's instructions.

Someone reviewing the agent now needs to understand how these pieces fit together. What capabilities are available? What does the prompt ask the model to do? Which rules are enforced by code, and what state do those rules depend on?

Modern agent frameworks provide middleware, callbacks, hooks, and plugins for implementing such behavior. I've been interested in a question about its organization: when an agent acquires its own application-specific logic, where should that logic live?

Could we treat the agent as a programmable object, with attributes, methods, and state, and keep its local rules alongside its definition? Shared implementations could still live in reusable modules, while the choices particular to this agent remain visible together.

From configurable agents to programmable objects

Consider an agent that examines support tickets and drafts replies using a knowledge-base search tool. Its role and initial capability can be described together:

description: "Examines one support ticket and drafts a reply."
tools:
  - search-knowledge

This declaration identifies the role and the search capability it uses. The search implementation can live elsewhere; reviewing the binding tells us which operation this agent can call.

Now suppose the application introduces another requirement:

Each ticket may use at most three knowledge-base searches. Once the budget is exhausted, the agent should use the evidence already collected or acknowledge what it cannot verify and request human assistance.

The agent needs a counter, a check before execution, and a way to handle the situation when another search is prohibited. The prompt can explain the intended behavior, while programmatic logic enforces the operational limit.

We could implement this through a tool wrapper, middleware, or application code. What makes agent-owned logic appealing here is the boundary between the search capability and the rules governing its use.

The tool has a semantic scope: search the knowledge base and return relevant information. This support role's conditions for using it can evolve independently. VIP tickets might get five attempts; tickets already handed to human support might stop searching; failed searches might consume the budget differently in another application.

A framework-provided limit may cover a simple case. As the conditions become more specific to the role, I sometimes find it more natural to express them as an ordinary method:

def _can_search(self):
    if self.escalated:
        return False
    limit = 5 if self.ticket_type == "vip" else 3
    return self.state.search_count < limit

Here, ticket_type and escalated represent application information supplied or maintained for the agent. The method reads that information and its own search count to express a rule. A change to the rule can be made in Python without introducing a configuration keyword for every variation.

This example assumes one agent per ticket; a quota shared across workers would need a shared source of truth. The scope of the state should follow the scope of the rule.

We can certainly put rules about customer status and query limits inside the search tool. That choice couples a reusable knowledge lookup operation to the application's classification and budget policies. Different control rules may then lead to separate tool variants or additional policy branches around the same search implementation.

A version that distinguishes VIP tickets would also need that classification supplied, for example through an extra ticket_type argument. This argument serves the control policy; it contributes no information to the knowledge query itself. As more conditions are added, the tool's interface and implementation take on more of the surrounding application's concerns.

For this role, I would prefer to keep the search tool focused on knowledge retrieval. The application can supply ticket facts to the agent, and the agent can maintain its own attempt count and decide whether its policy permits another search. Those rules can evolve while the search capability remains reusable.

An agent can be declarative where appropriate and directly programmable where useful. But giving an agent its own logic leaves another decision: where should we organize that logic?

If the prompt, state initialization, rule, and execution callback are assembled in different places, a reviewer needs to follow their connections. I would like the agent's definition to remain a useful place for reading those related decisions together.

An idea inspired by Vue's Single-File Components

Vue's Single-File Components bring a component's template, script, and styles into one .vue file. They describe different aspects of the same component, and a change to one aspect often needs to be understood in relation to the others.

A component can also have its own state and functions while importing shared behavior from other modules. That combination appeals to me: local logic stays near the definition it belongs to, and reusable implementations retain their own scope.

I wondered whether a similar organization could work for agents. Their instructions, capability bindings, attributes, persistent state, methods, and hooks collectively determine how a particular role behaves. When checking a search-budget rule, for example, I would like to see its state and enforcement point near the instructions and capabilities it affects.

There are two choices here: allowing the agent to own methods and state, and keeping those methods and state near the rest of its definition. Together, they could give a reviewer a coherent unit to examine as the agent gains application-specific behavior.

Larger implementations can still extract shared functions and services. What I want to preserve is a clear place for understanding how this particular agent is put together.

This is what I've been calling semantic self-containment.

Semantic self-containment

To make that idea concrete, consider this call:

use_retry(self, max_retries=3)

Its implementation can involve error classification, hook registration, and backoff. Including that implementation in every agent would create duplication, but this call already communicates a behavioral choice: the agent enables a retry policy with a limit of three.

The choice is locally visible, while its implementation remains reusable. A tool binding works similarly. The declaration identifies which search capability this agent uses; following the reference gives us its implementation details when needed.

A local method serves a complementary purpose:

def _search_budget_exhausted(self):
    return self.state.search_count >= self.state.search_limit

Here the rule itself is short enough to inspect directly. It can sit beside the registration of the state it reads and the hook that uses its result.

Both forms help explain the agent: a meaningful call selects reusable behavior, and a local method expresses a rule particular to this role. A reviewer can inspect their relationship to the prompt and capability declarations in the same place.

By semantic self-containment, I mean keeping an agent's capabilities, state, policies, and local logic understandable together, while allowing reusable implementations to retain their own scope. A definition can depend on several modules and still make this agent's choices clear.

The quality of those abstractions matters. A vague call such as apply_policies(self, config) could conceal substantial behavior even inside a single file. Explicit bindings, meaningful names, and readable assembly are what make that file a useful unit of review.

I've been exploring this idea through semantic self-containment, inspired in part by Vue's Single-File Components. In my open-source Python agent runtime, Flowing, a reusable agent declaration provides a place for both capability bindings and local Python behavior. What interests me is whether that organization can keep a growing agent easy to review.

Putting the idea into practice: a support agent in Flowing

We can explore this organization by building the support agent's definition step by step. In Flowing, the .fya("flowing yaml") format brings declarative fields, instructions, and agent-specific Python logic into one file. That gives us a place to examine how a capability declaration, a rule, and its enforcement fit together.

Let's return to the support role. We want an agent that examines one ticket, searches for relevant information, and drafts a reply. We'll implement the three-search budget directly so we can follow its state, methods, and hooks together. Then we can consider how further requirements fit into the same definition.

The search engine remains external. The surrounding application supplies ticket information and handles actual delivery and handoff. The part we are organizing here is the behavior specific to the support agent.

The following sections build the same support.fya. It begins with YAML fields, followed by named sections separated by ---: $system_prompt contains the instructions, and $script contains Python code. The initialization snippets belong to one setup() function.

1. Make the role and initial capability visible

A .fya is a reusable Agent declaration. We begin with a description and one tool binding:

description: "Examines one support ticket and drafts a reply."
tools:
  - search-knowledge

The tool list binds the operation the model can call. The application supplies its implementation; this file records that the support role uses it. A reviewer has a starting point for understanding the agent's purpose and capability.

2. Keep the instructions beside the capabilities

The next section describes how the model should perform that role:

---
$system_prompt:
You examine support ticket {{ticket_id}} and draft a reply.
Use verified knowledge-base information.
Do not invent policies, order details, or unsupported facts.

You have a limited search budget. When a search is blocked, use the
available evidence or explain what cannot be verified and request
human assistance.

The system prompt can also contain Jinja2 template expressions. Here, {{ticket_id}} is filled from the Agent's ticket_id attribute when context is assembled; the setup() function below supplies that attribute. The same definition can therefore serve different ticket instances.

The instructions explain how to use the search capability: collect evidence, draft a grounded reply, and acknowledge gaps when the available information is insufficient. They can be read alongside the binding immediately above them.

The budget instruction also gives the model guidance about what to do when it cannot search again. We still need code to check the count and stop a prohibited call. That is where the agent's own methods and state enter the definition.

3. Give the Agent its own methods

The $script block can define ordinary instance methods. For this policy, one method checks the budget and another provides the guidance to return when it is exhausted. setup() initializes the instance:

---
$script:
from flowing.errors import Intercepted


def _search_budget_exhausted(self):
    return self.state.search_count >= self.state.search_limit


def _fallback_instruction(self):
    return (
        "The search budget is exhausted. Use the available evidence "
        "or explain what cannot be verified and request human assistance."
    )


async def setup(self, ticket_id: str):
    self.ticket_id = ticket_id
    self.state.register("search_limit", 3)
    self.state.register("search_count", 0)

These functions become methods on the Agent object. They can read its attributes and state, and other methods or hooks can call them directly. The leading underscores are Python's convention for internal methods.

The ticket ID is an ordinary attribute supplied during initialization and used by the prompt template. The registered values are persistent state: the budget and the accumulated count.

Registration preserves a restored value instead of overwriting it with the default. That allows the agent to keep its accumulated count when the ticket continues across launches. The state registration and the method reading it are visible together, so their relationship can be reviewed without tracing a separate counter back to this instance.

4. Let a Hook enforce the rule

The methods need a point where they can affect execution. For this rule, that point is immediately before a search call. Inside the same setup(), attach a handler to that tool's pre-call hook:

    def limit_search(agent, call):
        if agent._search_budget_exhausted():
            raise Intercepted(agent._fallback_instruction())
        agent.state.search_count += 1
        return call

    self.hooks.before_tool_call["search-knowledge"](limit_search)

The handler receives the Agent and the pending call. It checks the agent's method, increments the counter when the call is allowed, and returns the call so execution can proceed. The name in the subscription scopes this handler to search-knowledge.

Raising Intercepted prevents execution and returns the reason to the model as a blocked tool result. The counter is incremented before execution, so an admitted call consumes an attempt even if execution subsequently fails.

The method, its state, and the enforcement point now appear together. A reviewer can see what the rule means and where it takes effect, while the search implementation retains its separate responsibility.

5. Intervene after the final search

The pre-call check blocks an attempt beyond the limit. We may also want to guide the model immediately after its final permitted attempt finishes, before it tries another search. To send that guidance once, we can register a notice flag and attach a second hook inside the same setup():

    self.state.register("budget_notice_sent", False)

    async def notify_limit(agent, result):
        if (
            agent._search_budget_exhausted()
            and not agent.state.budget_notice_sent
        ):
            agent.state.budget_notice_sent = True
            await agent.steer(agent._fallback_instruction())
        return result

    self.hooks.after_tool_call["search-knowledge"](notify_limit)

This handler consults the same budget method and records that it has sent the guidance. The flag avoids repeatedly sending that notice. steer() supplies it for a subsequent model call in the active turn; it does not interrupt an in-flight request.

The two hooks serve related purposes: the pre-call hook enforces the limit, and the post-call hook guides the model after the budget is consumed. Both can use the agent's own methods and state, and both are attached in the same declaration. That makes it possible to review the constraint and the behavior surrounding it together.

This example uses a search tool that returns its result normally. Background tools have separate result-delivery timing to consider.

Reusable behavior through Composables

Retrying a failed model request is useful across many roles. I would like to reuse that policy while keeping the choice to enable it visible in this agent.

A Composable is an ordinary Python function that attaches behavior to an Agent. For retries, import use_retry into $script and add its call to the existing setup():

from flowing.composables import use_retry

    use_retry(self, max_retries=3)

Like the search-budget handlers, this function uses the agent's hooks to intervene during execution. Its implementation is shared, while the decision to enable it and the configured limit are local to this definition.

I use the implementations in flowing.composables here as examples of what Composables can do. They express particular policy choices and may not be the best fit for a downstream application. Developers can use them as references, adapt them, or write their own Composables with the hooks, state, and methods their application needs. The behavior selected for an agent can still be made visible through an explicit call in its definition.

The same pattern can accommodate further requirements. Some reusable behaviors also need data describing what they should do. We can place that data in YAML and attach its consumer in setup(), keeping both choices visible together.

Procedure guidance through Skills

Suppose this agent now needs to follow delivery, refund, and escalation procedures maintained as separate documents. A Skill is a reusable document of task guidance that the agent can load when relevant.

We can extend the YAML with a skills field and add the loading tool to the existing tool list:

tools:
  - search-knowledge
  - skill-load
skills:
  - ./skills/delivery-support.md
  - ./skills/refund-handling.md
  - ./skills/human-escalation.md

Together with that data, import the corresponding Composable into $script and call it inside the existing setup():

from flowing.plugins.skills import use_skill

    use_skill(self)

skills is an ordinary, non-reserved field that becomes agent.skills. use_skill() reads it and assembles this instance's procedure catalog and loading methods. The extension also requires SkillPlugin to be installed on the Runtime; we will see that shared installation in the project entry point below.

Add the corresponding instruction to the existing system prompt:

Load the relevant Skill when handling delivery, refund, or
human-escalation questions.

A reviewer can inspect that instruction, the selected procedure documents, the loading-tool binding, and the call enabling the behavior in the same file.

Structured results for the host

Suppose the surrounding application also needs to distinguish a usable reply draft from a request for human assistance. A JSON result with named fields gives the host something it can consume programmatically.

We can describe the expected shape under another ordinary YAML field, output, and attach the Composable that checks it:

output:
  reply:
    type: string
    description: "Customer-facing reply draft."
  needs_human:
    type: boolean
    description: "Whether human assistance is required."
  reason:
    type: string
    description: "Reason for requesting human assistance, if any."

Import use_validate_turn_result into $script and add its call to the existing setup():

from flowing.composables import use_validate_turn_result

    use_validate_turn_result(self, on_fail="steer")

This function reads agent.output and registers a validation handler on the model-response hook. If the final response fails the schema check, on_fail="steer" supplies the validation feedback as a steering message and keeps the same turn running so the model can revise its response. The output contract is enforced by the attached behavior, including guidance toward a valid result.

The model also needs instructions to produce that result. Add to the existing system prompt:

Return JSON with reply (string), needs_human (boolean), and reason
(string). Set needs_human to true when human assistance is required.
Do not claim that a human handoff has already been completed.

A reviewer can now check the requested JSON, the expected shape, and the validator consuming it together. Both output and skills get their meaning from the code that reads them. Application-defined fields can follow the same pattern: each need introduces its data and the behavior using it, with reusable implementations remaining external.

From the Agent declaration to the host application

The support agent owns its search policy and produces a structured decision. The host runs it and performs the actual handoff.

A .fya defines an Agent class. The Runtime mounts it as a live object with its own attributes, state, hooks, and message history. One instance per ticket gives each ticket an independent search budget.

A project assembly function could look like this:

from flowing import Runtime
from flowing.plugins.skills import SkillPlugin
from app.support_tools import register_support_tools


async def main(ticket_id: str) -> Runtime:
    runtime = Runtime()
    runtime.set_model_tags("@/model-tags.yaml")
    runtime.install(SkillPlugin())
    register_support_tools(runtime)
    await runtime.mount(
        "@/support.fya", agent_id=f"ticket-{ticket_id}", ticket_id=ticket_id
    )
    return runtime

register_support_tools() represents application code registering the search implementation. The project supplies its Skill files and model configuration too. A stable Agent ID lets a later launch restore that ticket's messages and registered state. Normal shutdown drains pending persistence writes.

The host uses launch(project_dir, ticket_id=...), retrieves the Agent with get_agent(), and awaits agent.query(ticket_text). It handles an unsuccessful turn through its own fallback path. For a completed result, it consumes the validated JSON, reviews or delivers the draft, and acts on needs_human.

Requesting human assistance and completing a handoff are distinct operations. The application owns delivery and mandatory business escalation rules. Output validation establishes structure; it cannot establish that the model's judgment is correct.

Could this organization help coding agents?

Suppose the product team now asks for five searches on VIP tickets and no further searches after human handoff. A coding assistant modifying this agent has a natural starting point in support.fya: the state, budget method, fallback guidance, and hooks are locally visible.

It could introduce a method like _can_search() from the earlier example and have the hook consult it. Ticket classification and handoff status would need appropriate application sources, and the fallback guidance would need to cover both blocking conditions.

That makes the modification's related parts discoverable. It also exposes persistence questions: changing the default in state.register("search_limit", ...) preserves existing restored limits, so changing defaults and updating existing tickets are separate tasks.

I see a possible benefit here for coding assistants maintaining application-specific agents. Whether this organization improves modification accuracy would need evidence from actual tasks.

For humans: understanding, review, and monitoring

A human reviewing that change can examine the capability bindings, instructions, state registration, methods, and hook attachment together. The file provides a common point of reference for questions such as:

  • Where does VIP status come from, and who updates handoff status?
  • Is the constraint enforced, and does it count attempts or successes?
  • Which values survive recovery?
  • Does the output express the decision the host expects?

External implementations still need review where relevant. The declaration makes their relationship to this particular agent easier to follow.

Runtime observations can complement that static view. A hook can record the count, the decision, and agent.node_id at the point where it permits or blocks a search. The host can also inspect the live Agent's state and message history. Those observations help connect the rule being reviewed to what happened during execution.

Keeping related behavior nearby may make it easier to check consistency across code, instructions, and observations. Its usefulness depends on the quality of those abstractions and on the surrounding application.

Where I would draw the boundary

The convenience of writing methods and hooks directly in an agent definition can make it tempting to keep adding code there. I would use that flexibility while it keeps the agent's behavior easy to review. Keeping everything in one file can become a goal of its own, at the expense of that clarity.

For a small agent-specific rule, a method and a few hooks can be the clearest organization. As the implementation grows or more roles share the rule, extracting a Composable may improve understanding and reuse. Its invocation and parameters can remain in the declaration, so the agent's choice of behavior stays visible.

Responsibilities also need to retain their proper scope. A search engine can stay in a tool, detailed procedures in Skills, and application-wide workflows in the host. A quota shared by several workers needs a shared control point; placing a separate counter on every Agent would not enforce that quota. The ability to put logic on an Agent does not make it the right owner of every rule.

The same restraint applies to file size. A declaration crowded with unrelated implementation details can become harder to review than a few well-organized modules. I would extract those details when doing so makes the agent easier to understand, leaving its bindings, policy choices, and agent-specific logic together. That is the boundary I want to preserve: the file remains a coherent entry point for reviewing the agent's behavior.

After appropriate extraction, the definition can still be semantically self-contained. It can show which behaviors the agent adopts, how they are configured, and how they fit together, while encapsulating implementation details in external modules. A call such as use_retry(self, max_retries=3) makes the policy choice and limit visible while leaving hook registration and backoff details elsewhere. Those details may require following the reference, but the agent's behavioral assembly remains locally understandable.

Trade-offs and open questions

A programmable .fya contains executable application code. Its external tools, shared policies, and host-side hooks can all affect runtime behavior. Reviewing the file remains part of a broader process involving dependency review, testing, and observation.

An ordinary Python class can also collect related logic. Flowing supports handwritten Agent subclasses alongside .fya; both produce the same class model. The file format gives declarations, long prompts, and Python methods a common authoring structure that I am exploring as a default unit of review.

Other frameworks already offer state, middleware, hooks, plugins, and callbacks. The choice I am exploring is to make the reusable Agent definition a consistent place for discovering an agent's capabilities, policies, and application-specific logic.

For some applications, ordinary Python construction or a more distributed organization may be clearer. The useful question is how well the chosen boundary supports understanding as requirements accumulate.

Conclusion: a possible programming boundary for Agents

The support agent began with capabilities and instructions. Its search policy brought persistent state, methods, execution constraints, and fallback behavior into that definition. Keeping these related pieces together gives a reviewer a coherent place to examine how the role works.

That is the value I hope semantic self-containment can offer: one file where an agent's selected capabilities and its own behavioral rules can be reviewed together, with reusable implementations retaining their own scope.

I'm exploring this approach in Flowing. Its documentation covers declarations, hooks, Composables, and embedding the runtime in Python applications.

When reviewing an agent with application-specific logic, which parts of its behavior do you want to see together, and when does extracting a rule into another module make that review easier?

If this approach resonates with you, give Flowing a try. I'd love to hear what you build with it—and if you like the idea, a star on GitHub would mean a lot.

title: OpenAI Brings In Ex-DOGE Startup Cathedral to Attack Its Own Systems, Bug Bounties Hit $172K
description:
Originally published on Rohan Tech Official.

OpenAI just hired a company to break into OpenAI. On November 2, the company announced that Cathedral Systems — an AI security startup founded by ex-DOGE staffers — will join its next internal security sprint, using OpenAI's own models to attack its defenses. At the same time, OpenAI more than quadrupled its bug bounties, with top payouts reaching $172,000.

Why would the world's most-watched AI lab invite hackers inside? Because the threats are getting smarter — and so are the defenses it needs.

Who Is Cathedral?

Cathedral Systems is a young AI security startup with an unusual pedigree: its founders are former staffers from DOGE, the government efficiency outfit. But the detail that turned heads came from the Washington Post, which reported that Cathedral's AI agents got inside Anthropic's internal systems in October — one of the most security-conscious AI labs on the planet.

That's quite a calling card. If your agents can breach Anthropic, every other AI company wants to know how you did it — ideally before someone with worse intentions figures it out. For more on OpenAI's recent moves, see our coverage of the ChatGPT Codex single shared plan.

Attacking OpenAI With Its Own Models

Here's the twist that makes this sprint genuinely interesting: Cathedral won't just throw human red-teamers at OpenAI's infrastructure. It will use OpenAI's own models to attack OpenAI's defenses. AI agents probing AI systems, hunting for weaknesses at machine speed.

This is where AI security is heading. Human testers are thorough but slow; AI agents can try thousands of attack paths in the time it takes a person to write one report. The same agentic capabilities that make AI useful — planning, tool use, persistence — make it a formidable attacker. OpenAI is essentially stress-testing its fortress with an army that thinks like the enemy.

Bug Bounties, Quadrupled

Alongside the Cathedral announcement, OpenAI massively raised the stakes for independent researchers. Critical vulnerabilities in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API now pay up to $30,000. Exceptional findings start at a $100,000 base — and with quality, loyalty, and campaign bonuses, top payouts can reach $172,000.

That's more than four times the previous rewards, and it puts OpenAI's program among the most generous in tech. The message to the security community is unmistakable: we want your best work, and we'll pay for it. Researchers can find the full details on OpenAI's Bugcrowd page or through OpenAI's official site.

Why Now?

Timing is everything. AI systems are becoming more capable, more autonomous, and more deeply embedded in critical workflows — which means the consequences of a breach keep growing. An attacker who compromises a frontier model's training pipeline or deployment infrastructure doesn't just steal data; they could poison the model itself.

The Cathedral-Anthropic episode in October likely focused minds. When a startup's agents can penetrate a top-tier lab, it proves the threat model has changed. Human red teams alone can't keep up with agentic attacks — you need agentic defenses, tested by agentic attackers. The Anthropic text watermark story showed how seriously labs take integrity; this sprint shows how seriously they take security.

What This Tells Us About AI Security

Three takeaways. First, the AI security market is maturing fast — startups like Cathedral can now sell "our agents broke into Anthropic" as a credential. Second, the line between AI capability research and AI security research is dissolving; the same agents that do useful work can do harmful work, and defending against them requires understanding both.

Third, money talks. A $172K top bounty will pull elite researchers toward AI targets and away from traditional software. Expect the next year to surface vulnerabilities in AI systems that nobody has thought to look for yet — because until now, nobody was paying enough to look.

What's Next

The sprint itself will run behind closed doors, and OpenAI will decide what to disclose. Watch for two things: whether the bounty program produces headline findings in the coming months, and whether other labs copy the playbook.

If Cathedral's agents find real holes in OpenAI's defenses, that's a win for everyone who uses these systems. The uncomfortable alternative — that nobody looked — is no longer an option.

title: A finished revision can still leave a stale review copy
description:
A technical article had been revised locally, and the completion record contained the revised file's hash. The cloud copy provided for review still contained the earlier draft.

The URL had not changed. That did not establish which text it contained. Comparing the local revision and the review copy as separate artifacts revealed the mismatch.

A filename and a URL do not identify the revision

In the saved records from October 20, 2026, the revised local draft was 5,387 bytes. The review copy was 3,171 bytes. The revision added information about the verification scope, while the review copy retained the earlier explanation.

The entire review text matched the preserved old draft. The current local manuscript matched the SHA-256 recorded when the revision was completed.

Those checks established two different states: the local revision existed, and the delivered copy matched the old draft. An accessible URL and an unchanged filename did not distinguish them.

Separate the original, the intended snapshot, and the readback

For this UTF-8 Markdown workflow, three artifacts have different jobs:

Artifact Purpose
Working original The document that can continue to change
Manuscript snapshot The exact text intended for this handoff
Text read back from the review copy An observation of what the destination contains

After updating the review copy, the readback string was encoded as UTF-8 and compared with every byte of the manuscript snapshot. The reported stored size was also 5,387 bytes, and the SHA-256 values matched.

The simplified check looks like this. This is explanatory pseudocode with the retrieval API and error handling omitted, not a newly validated distribution tool.

expected = bytes of the manuscript snapshot intended for review
observed = complete review-copy text encoded as UTF-8

Check every byte of observed against expected
Compare the reported stored size with the length of expected
Record the SHA-256 of the compared text and the check time

This evidence is a comparison of retrieved UTF-8 text and reported size. It should not be described as a separate raw binary download test of the cloud file.

Check history and sharing separately from content

Before the update, the existing review text was checked against the preserved old draft. The content was then updated under the same file ID. No new public link or sharing destination was created.

The saved records show that the filename, ID, parent location, and nonshared permission state remained unchanged. They also show more than an old revision appearing in a history list: that revision was read back and its complete text matched the preserved old manuscript.

That establishes that the earlier revision was readable at the time of the operation. It does not promise indefinite history retention. The comparison before writing is also not an atomic lock. Safe handling of an edit arriving between the comparison and the write was not established.

If the destination differs from the preserved draft in an unexpected way, there is insufficient evidence to call it merely stale and replace it. Preserve both versions and resolve which one should be used. Avoiding automatic resends after an uncertain outcome is an operational rule here, not the result of a network-fault injection test.

Text identity is not factual review or publication approval

A hash or full-text comparison helps identify what was handed over. It does not establish that the claims are correct, that the prose is clear, or that the author has approved publication.

For this article, I rechecked the saved October 20 operation records and readback text against the manuscripts retained locally. This is not a fresh inspection of the current cloud document. The development tests discussed in the underlying manuscript were not rerun either.

Revising the original does not prove that the review copy was updated. Linking the intended snapshot to the text read back from its destination made that handoff mismatch observable and allowed it to be resolved in this case.

AI assisted the operation's comparison process, the organization of the saved records, and the organization and writing of this article.

title: AI Support Automation vs BPO Outsourcing: 2026 Cost, Speed & Quality Breakdown
description:
AI is cheaper and faster for simple, repeatable questions. Outsourcing customer service to a BPO is still better value for complex, emotional, or phone-heavy work.

This guide compares the two on 2026 prices, speed, and quality, and shows when a hybrid of both costs least.

1. The Short Answer

AI support automation costs less than customer service outsourcing for high-volume, simple questions, but a BPO team still wins on complex, sensitive, and voice-heavy work. Most mid-size companies get the lowest total cost by combining them.

Human contacts keep getting more expensive. Deloitte Digital’s 2026 Global Contact Center Survey puts the average cost of an assisted contact at $7.80, up from $6.70 in 2024. AI is not a free alternative either. Gartner expects generative AI to cost more than $3 per resolution by 2030, above many offshore human agents.

Key takeaways

  • Offshore BPO support typically costs $5 to $16 per agent hour in India and the Philippines in 2026, before setup, tools, and management.
  • AI agents are often priced per resolution. Intercom lists Fin at $0.99 per outcome, and unresolved conversations still need a person.
  • Gartner forecasts generative AI will cost more than $3 per resolution by 2030, so do not assume AI prices only fall.
  • AI wins on speed and 24/7 coverage. People win on complaints, judgement, and trust.
  • For most mid-size teams, a hybrid of AI for simple questions and a smaller BPO team costs least.

2. What Does Customer Service Outsourcing Cost in 2026?

Most BPO contracts charge per agent hour or per dedicated agent per month. Location sets most of the price. Published 2026 rate cards from outsourcing providers cluster in these ranges for customer support:

  • India and the Philippines: $5 to $16 per agent hour.
  • Latin America: $12 to $24 per agent hour.
  • United States: $28 to $42 per agent hour.

These are vendor estimates, not audited benchmarks.

The hourly rate is only part of the bill. You also pay for setup and training, quality checks, the help desk and phone tools, and your own team managing the vendor. BPOs bill for idle time too, so an agent waiting for the next ticket costs the same as one solving it.

Note: Agent turnover is a hidden cost. Contact center attrition is high, and each new agent needs training before reaching full speed, so you keep paying for ramp-up.

3. What Does AI Customer Service Cost?

AI customer service is usually priced per resolution or per conversation. Intercom lists its Fin AI agent at $0.99 per outcome. Other vendors charge per conversation, per seat, or a flat platform fee. Custom builds swap the usage fee for build and running costs.

The fee per resolution is not the full cost. You also pay for:

  • Setup and integration with your systems.
  • Writing and maintaining the knowledge base the AI answers from.
  • Monitoring answer quality.
  • The humans who take over when the AI cannot help.

Gartner’s January 2026 forecast is a useful warning. It cites rising data center costs, vendors moving from subsidised growth to profit, and more complex use cases. Our view: model AI cost per resolution as flat or rising over a three-year contract, not falling.

4. AI vs. BPO: Cost, Speed and Quality Compared

The table compares an AI agent with an offshore BPO team on the points that usually decide the contract.

  • Pricing model: AI is billed per resolution, per conversation, or as a platform fee. A BPO bills per agent hour or per dedicated agent a month.
  • Cost on simple questions: AI is lowest once set up, around $1 per resolution at list price. A BPO charges the same hourly rate whether the question is simple or hard.
  • Cost on complex cases: AI often fails and hands off, so you pay twice. Trained BPO agents resolve in one contact.
  • Speed: AI replies in seconds, 24/7, with no queue at peaks. A BPO depends on staffing, and night and weekend shifts cost more.
  • Scaling for a peak: AI is instant, and cost rises with volume. A BPO needs weeks to hire and train extra agents.
  • Quality and empathy: AI is consistent on documented answers and weak on upset customers. BPO quality varies with training and agent turnover.
  • Setup time: AI takes weeks for a help desk add-on and months for a custom build. A BPO typically takes weeks to months for hiring and training.
  • Control of data: AI data stays in your systems if self-hosted or contracted that way. With a BPO, third-party staff access customer data.

Speed is where AI clearly leads. It answers in seconds at any hour, and volume spikes do not create a queue. A BPO needs weeks to hire and train for a new peak, and night shifts cost more.

5. AI vs. BPO Cost Calculator

Enter your volume and rates to compare three setups: BPO only, AI only for what it can resolve, and a hybrid where AI takes the simple share and the BPO handles the rest.

Worked example with the design’s default inputs: 10,000 conversations a month, 8 minutes per conversation for a human agent, a BPO rate of $12 an hour, 40% of conversations resolved by AI and $0.99 per AI resolution. BPO only costs about $21,333 a month, or $2.13 per conversation. A hybrid costs about $16,760, or $1.68 per conversation, because AI resolves 4,000 conversations and the BPO handles the other 6,000. That is a saving of about $4,573 a month, 21% less than BPO only.

The calculator assumes 75% agent occupancy and that every conversation the AI does not resolve goes to the BPO. It excludes setup, tools, knowledge upkeep and vendor management on both sides, so treat it as an illustration. To weigh software cost against hours saved, try the free AI ROI Calculator on https://neuradynamics.ai/.

Tip: Run the numbers with your real resolution rate from a pilot, not a vendor’s headline figure. Each conversation the AI fails to resolve still costs you a human contact.

6. Which Gives Better Quality, AI or Human Agents?

It depends on the question. AI is consistent on factual answers it has a source for, such as order status, policies and how-to steps. People do better when the customer is upset, the case needs judgement, or the answer is not written down anywhere.

Customers say the same. In a Gartner survey of 5,801 US customers, 54% trusted human agents more than AI for product or service recommendations, against 32% who trusted AI more. A separate 2026 Gartner survey found 87% of customers say access to a human agent is essential when companies use generative AI.

  • AI alone (simple and documented): order status and tracking, password and login help, policy and how-to questions.
  • AI drafts, person approves (needs a check): refunds and credits, plan and billing changes, warranty claims.
  • People, in-house or BPO (judgement and trust): complaints and escalations, cancellations and retention, complex technical cases.

7. How to Move From BPO to a Hybrid Model in 5 Steps

Most companies we speak to do not replace their BPO outright. They shift the simple share of volume to AI and renegotiate the contract around what is left.

  1. Tag a month of tickets by intent. Mark which ones a written answer could resolve. This share sets your AI ceiling.
  2. Price both sides. Use the calculator above with your real BPO rate and handle time.
  3. Pilot AI on the top intents. Run it on one channel for four to six weeks and measure true resolution, not just deflection.
  4. Renegotiate the BPO contract. Shift from fixed seats to the reduced, more complex volume. Ask for pricing per resolved case where possible.
  5. Review monthly. Track cost per resolution, customer satisfaction and handoff rate for AI and BPO side by side.

Gartner’s research suggests this is the common path. In its survey of 321 service leaders, 85% were expanding human agent responsibilities as AI took on simple work.

8. Real Examples

Klarna: AI first, then people again

In February 2024, Klarna reported that its AI assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, two-thirds of its service chats, and cut resolution time from 11 minutes to under 2. It said the assistant did the work of 700 full-time agents.

In May 2025, its CEO told Bloomberg the company was hiring human agents again so customers could always reach a person. The AI stayed on routine questions. The lesson for anyone replacing a BPO: cut the simple volume, not the human option.

Two of our builds

For a payments company, we built an omnichannel customer support system that answers high-confidence email queries in under a minute and hands complex cases to human support with context. For ecommerce merchants, we built an AI assistant that drafts replies from live order data, with an agent approving each one.

  • Paymate: under 1 minute first response on high-confidence email queries, down from hours, with complex cases handed to human support.
  • Zenva: ~50 hours saved per month, an estimate for one store with 2,000 customer emails a month. AI drafts replies from order data and an agent approves each one.

9. Common Mistakes

  • Comparing an AI list price with a fully loaded BPO cost. Add setup, knowledge upkeep and human fallback to the AI side too.
  • Counting deflection as resolution. A customer who leaves the chat and calls later is not resolved.
  • Cancelling the BPO before the AI is proven. Run both through a full peak season first.
  • Hiding the route to a person. Gartner expects regulation on access to humans to raise assisted volume 30% by 2028.
  • Signing long AI contracts on today’s prices. Gartner forecasts AI cost per resolution to rise, so cap price increases in the contract.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

Is AI customer service cheaper than outsourcing?

For simple, documented questions, usually yes. AI agents list at around $1 per resolution, while an offshore BPO agent costs $5 to $16 an hour. For complex cases AI often hands off, so you pay for both. Gartner also forecasts AI cost per resolution will exceed $3 by 2030.

How much does customer service outsourcing cost?

Published 2026 rate guides put customer support outsourcing at about $5 to $16 per agent hour in India and the Philippines, $12 to $24 in Latin America and $28 to $42 in the US. Setup, training, tools and vendor management are extra. Rates vary with language, channel and contract length.

Can AI replace a BPO call center?

Rarely in full. AI handles high-volume, simple questions well, but customers still want people for complaints and complex cases. Klarna moved much of its chat volume to AI in 2024, then began hiring human agents again in 2025. Most companies shrink the BPO contract instead of ending it.

What is the difference between BPO and AI support automation?

BPO outsourcing means paying another company’s staff to handle your customer conversations, usually per hour or per agent. AI support automation uses software to answer customers directly, usually priced per resolution or conversation. A hybrid model uses AI for simple questions and people for the rest.

Which is faster, AI or a BPO team?

AI. It replies in seconds at any hour and does not queue during spikes. A BPO team’s speed depends on how many agents are scheduled, and adding capacity for a peak takes weeks of hiring and training. For phone support, a well-staffed BPO can still answer quickly.

How do I calculate AI vs BPO cost?

Multiply monthly conversations by handle time in hours, divide by agent occupancy and multiply by the BPO hourly rate. For AI, multiply resolved conversations by the price per resolution, then add the human cost of the rest. Compare total cost per conversation, not list prices.

11. Conclusion

Choosing between AI support automation and customer service outsourcing comes down to what your customers ask. Pull last quarter’s tickets, mark which ones follow a written answer, and price that share at an AI rate and the rest at your BPO rate. If the simple share is large, a hybrid will almost always beat either option alone.
