  "planner": "deepseek-v4-pro",
  "executor": "deepseek-v4-flash"
}

The CLI uses that pair only if both models are in the catalog it just loaded. Otherwise it falls back to its built-in pair. So I can swap the planner on the server without shipping a new CLI.

When to use it

Fusion fits tasks where a bad plan costs you more than a slow start:

  • Changes that touch several files.
  • A feature plus the tests for it.
  • Refactors where the order of steps matters.

For a one-line fix, plain DeepSeek V4 Flash is usually the better pick. Under Fusion, even a tiny edit waits for exploration and a planning request.

Trade-offs

  • The plan request costs more. Pro is the more expensive model, so its request uses more of your daily allowance than a Flash request. The /model picker shows how fast each model uses it.
  • Prompt caches don't carry over. pi's docs say switching models loses the prompt cache. Each switch between Flash and Pro sends the context without it.
  • Shell commands aren't blocked. Exploration needs bash, so Fusion leaves it alone. A shell command can still change files before the plan exists. Keep your work in git.
  • One plan per message. Pro writes the plan once. If the build goes sideways, send a new message and Fusion starts over from explore.

Wrapping up

Fusion is a small router on top of pi. Flash explores, Pro writes one plan into the todo list, and Flash builds it. Edits stay blocked until the plan exists, and failures fall back to Flash instead of stalling. Use it for multi-file work, and stay on Flash for quick fixes.

Try it free with npx free-pi-cli@latest, pick Fusion in /model, and read more at www.freepi.ai.

title: 11 tools in my MCP server, 3 of them did 91% of the calls: what I ask before adding a 12th
description:
Two weeks ago the MCP server behind my orchestrator exposed 11 tools. It exposes 4 now. Nothing the agent does changed, because three of those 11 were already doing 91% of the work and I had never bothered to count.

The orchestrator is a small thing I run for content operations: it plans slots, drafts copy, schedules what passes review. Every step talks to the same MCP server, which I maintain, which means every bad decision in it is mine. I went looking because of the token bill. I stayed because of the errors.

What the log said

I turned on one structured line per tool call and left it for 16 days. 427 runs, 1,318 calls.

jq -r 'select(.event=="tool_call") | .tool' calls.ndjson \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

    612 get_content_brief
    402 save_draft
    187 list_pending_slots
     54 get_brand_voice
     33 publish_draft
     18 schedule_post
      7 get_channel_stats
      3 search_published
      2 update_slot_status

Nine lines for eleven tools. archive_draft and get_competitor_feed never showed up at all, which is the kind of absence uniq -c will never tell you about. The top three add up to 1,201 of 1,318 calls, a bit over 91%.

All eleven definitions ride along in every request. I ran the tool block through the tokenizer the model actually uses and got a bit over 6,400 tokens. The three tools doing the work account for about 1,900 of those. So on each of those 1,318 calls I paid to re-send roughly 4,500 tokens of JSON schema describing tools the model mostly ignored. Somewhere near 5.9 million tokens of context spent on a menu.

Then the failures. 37 calls came back with argument validation errors, and 29 of them were the model reaching for publish_draft when it meant schedule_post, or the reverse. I put the two descriptions side by side and I would have gotten it wrong too.

[
  { "name": "publish_draft",  "description": "Publish a draft to its channel." },
  { "name": "schedule_post",  "description": "Publish a draft to its channel at a given time." }
]

The second one is the first one with an extra argument. Blaming the model for that is cheap.

I am not the only person running this math this month. A post here about cutting an MCP server from 15 tools to 4 pulled 76 comments against 61 reactions, a ratio you almost never see on this site, and more argument than applause usually means nobody agrees on where the line goes. InfoQ reported this week that Uber put a gateway in front of more than 800 MCP servers and over 5,000 tools, with incremental discovery so an agent never sees the whole catalogue at once. Same problem, four orders of magnitude up.

The fix I tried first and threw away

My first move was the clever one: collapse everything into a single call tool with an action string and a free-form payload, dispatched server side. The tool block dropped to a little over 300 tokens and I was briefly very pleased with myself.

Then the agent started inventing actions. create_brief. draft_save. Names that read exactly like my own convention and did not exist. Across 90 runs, something like 1 in 6 calls needed a retry, because an enum the model cannot see is an enum the model will guess. The schema was not overhead, it was the contract. I put it back and went after the list instead.

The three questions

Does it write? Then what undoes it?

Every write tool in the registry has to name the tool that reverses it, as a required field. If I cannot name the inverse, the agent does not get the tool. That killed archive_draft in about four seconds: the unarchive was me running an UPDATE by hand, which is not an undo the agent can reach.

type ToolSpec = {
  name: string;
  mode: "read" | "write";
  undo?: string;      // required when mode === "write"
  owner: string;      // a person, not a team alias
  secret?: string;    // credential id this tool uses
  rotatedAt?: string;
};

for (const t of tools) {
  if (t.mode === "write" && !t.undo) {
    throw new Error(`write tool ${t.name} has no documented undo`);
  }
  if (t.mode === "write" && !t.owner) {
    throw new Error(`write tool ${t.name} has no owner`);
  }
}

It fails at boot, not at runtime. The secret and rotatedAt fields are there for the question nobody asks until something leaks: each tool is a credential with a blast radius, and an agent that holds nine of them holds nine keys. Mine had two tools sharing one API key whose last rotation I could not date.

Reading only the descriptions, would I pick the right one?

Hide the names, read the one-liners, choose. If two tools differ only by an argument, they are one tool. publish_draft and schedule_post became one publish_draft with an optional at. Over the following 16 days, wrong-tool errors went from 37 to 3, and two of those three were my planner sending a bad payload.

This is the question that pays fastest, and it costs nothing but reading your own manifest as a stranger would.

Does it earn its schema?

Calls per week against tokens of definition, every request, forever. get_channel_stats: 7 calls in 16 days, around 480 tokens riding along 1,318 times. It did not earn it.

None of the deleted tools disappeared. They moved behind a second call. list_capabilities returns names and one-line summaries, and the full schema for a group arrives only when the agent asks for it. The planning step sees 4 tools. The rare paths pay their own cost at the moment they are used, which is the same trick Uber's gateway does with a much bigger catalogue.

Where it landed

Four tools in the default surface: get_content_brief, save_draft, list_pending_slots, publish_draft. Tool block down from a bit over 6,400 tokens to about 2,050. Wrong-tool errors from 37 to 3 over a comparable window. The agent has asked for the discovery group 9 times in 16 days, and get_competitor_feed is still at zero, so it will probably come out of the registry entirely.

One number I will not claim: latency. The p50 of the planning step went from around 9s to under 7s, but I changed the tool list and the prompt in the same week, so attributing that to the schema would be a story, not a measurement.

And one thing I genuinely do not know how to scale. The undo rule works because the registry has one maintainer. With nine teams publishing tools into a shared gateway, somebody is going to type undo: "manual" and move on, and the boot assertion will pass while the guarantee quietly stops existing.

So: hard cap on the default surface, or discovery from day one? And what do you do with a write tool whose only inverse is a human with database access?

Originally published on the Revin blog.

title: Valid JSON, Wrong Order: Five Structured-Output Myths and a Three-Gate Replay Test
description:
A pipeline of mine broke last week. Not on a timeout. Not on a 500.

It broke because the model returned 'quantity': '3'. A string. Twelve downstream orders went out with a quantity of zero.

So let me ask the boring question. Would your tests have caught that? Mine did not, and I wrote them.

Here are five claims I keep hearing about structured output. Each one comes with evidence you can collect yourself, and a corrected mental model.

Myth 1: JSON mode means my schema is enforced

No. It means the bytes parse as JSON. That is a syntax promise, not a contract.

I keep seeing this confusion in reviews. Someone enables a JSON flag and deletes the validator. Type drift then walks straight into the database.

Evidence you can collect in ten minutes: save 50 raw responses, then run them through json.loads. Count the parses. Then run the parses through a real schema validator. The two numbers will differ.

Corrected model: JSON mode protects the parser. Your schema protects the domain.

Myth 2: If it parses, the model was right

Parsing is the cheapest gate. It is also the least informative.

The output can parse, match the schema, and still be business-wrong. Totals that do not add up. A status the state machine never allows. An order id from another tenant.

Corrected model: validation has three layers, not one.

  1. Gate A: does it parse?
  2. Gate B: does it match the schema?
  3. Gate C: does it survive your cross-field rules?

Most teams ship gate A and call it done. That is where my string '3' came from.

Myth 3: Retrying fixes bad output

Retrying with the same prompt is a coin flip. Sometimes it lands. You learn nothing either way.

Ask yourself what the retry actually changed. If the answer is nothing, you bought variance, not reliability.

Before you add a retry loop, measure your gate failure rate. If gate B fails 4% of the time, a retry hides it. It does not remove it. And you still cannot explain the 4%.

Corrected model: retries are a mitigation. The gate is the fix.

Myth 4: Strict mode enforces my constraints

Strict modes vary by provider. Some enforce types well. Fewer enforce regex patterns, ranges, or cross-field arithmetic.

Can your validator tell the difference between absent and null? Does it reject booleans where you expect integers? In Python, isinstance(True, int) is true. That bites people.

Corrected model: treat generated constraints as hints. Treat your validator as law.

Myth 5: Schema drift is a model problem

It is a contract problem. You version your API. Version your output schema too.

When a prompt changes and the field list changes with it, you have a silent breaking change. Nothing alerts. Nothing fails loudly.

Corrected model: the schema lives in version control, next to the prompt. It has a version number. The gate logs that version with every rejection.

The three-gate check

Here is the gate I use. It is a template, not a benchmark. I have run it on my own traffic; your failure mix will differ.

# gate.py
import json
from collections import Counter
from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator

SCHEMA = {
    '$schema': 'https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema',
    'type': 'object',
    'required': ['order_id', 'quantity', 'unit_cents', 'total_cents', 'status'],
    'additionalProperties': False,
    'properties': {
        'order_id':    {'type': 'string', 'pattern': '^ord_[0-9a-f]{8}$'},
        'quantity':    {'type': 'integer', 'minimum': 1, 'maximum': 999},
        'unit_cents':  {'type': 'integer', 'minimum': 0},
        'total_cents': {'type': 'integer', 'minimum': 0},
        'status':      {'type': 'string', 'enum': ['new', 'paid', 'shipped']},
    },
}

VALIDATOR = Draft202012Validator(SCHEMA)
COUNT = Counter()

def gate_a(raw):
    try:
        return json.loads(raw), None
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        COUNT['gateA'] += 1
        return None, 'gateA:not-json@%d' % e.pos

def gate_b(obj):
    errors = sorted(VALIDATOR.iter_errors(obj), key=lambda e: list(e.path))
    if errors:
        path = '/'.join(str(p) for p in errors[0].path) or '$'
        COUNT['gateB'] += 1
        return None, 'gateB:schema:' + path
    return obj, None

def gate_c(obj):
    if obj['total_cents'] != obj['quantity'] * obj['unit_cents']:
        COUNT['gateC:arithmetic'] += 1
        return None, 'gateC:total-mismatch'
    return obj, None

Three functions. Three failure counters. That is the whole idea.

One nuance: coerce before you reject. '3' can become 3. But log the coercion. A rising coercion rate is a prompt regression, and you want to see it.

The replay harness

You do not need a live model to test this. Save raw responses, then replay them.

# replay.py  — expects JSONL where each line is {'content': '<raw model output>'}
import json, sys
from gate import gate_a, gate_b, gate_c, COUNT

kept = 0
with open(sys.argv[1], encoding='utf-8') as fh:
    for line in fh:
        raw = json.loads(line)['content']
        obj, err = gate_a(raw)
        if err:
            continue
        obj, err = gate_b(obj)
        if err:
            continue
        obj, err = gate_c(obj)
        if err:
            continue
        kept += 1

print('kept', kept, dict(COUNT))

Run it like this:

python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install jsonschema
python replay.py saved_responses.jsonl

Now the output is a number you can argue about. Not a vibe.

Decision table

Failed gate Likely cause Action
A (parse) truncation, markdown fence raise output budget, strip fences
B (schema) type drift, extra field tighten prompt, pin schema version
B (schema) missing field make it required, give a default in code
C (semantics) model did arithmetic compute totals in code
C (semantics) guessed enum value ask for inputs, derive the state

That last row matters. Stop asking the model to do arithmetic. Ask for quantity and unit_cents. Multiply in code.

Running the gate next to the model

Here is the practical part. The gate should sit in the same process as the model call. Network hops cost latency. Latency costs retries.

That is why I keep the gate script on the same box as the model call. If you are trying this with free model access, MonkeyCode describes a free server option that lets you co-locate them. The offer described to me is free model access with a token allowance reported as 10 million tokens, plus that free server option. Quotas change, so check the live page before you plan around a number.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The free tier is fine for the replay loop. It is a poor place for a p99 latency claim. Do not confuse the two.

Limitations you should hear

  • The gate catches contract violations, not hallucinations. A field can be valid and still wrong.
  • Gate C is domain code. It will never be generic, and it should not be.
  • My replay numbers are not published here because they are my traffic. Replay your own.
  • Schema libraries differ on format support. Test the validator, not just the model.

Who should not use this

Skip the three-gate design if your SDK already enforces a typed contract end to end. Skip it if your output is prose for humans, with no downstream consumer. Skip it if you cannot store raw responses, because then replay is impossible.

Also skip it if you plan to hide gate failures behind retries. That defeats the point.

A five-minute checklist

  1. Save 50 raw model responses today.
  2. Write the schema. Add additionalProperties: False.
  3. Run the replay. Write down three numbers.
  4. Add one gate C rule. Just one.
  5. Re-run. Compare.

So what does your schema actually guarantee? If the answer is only that the bytes parse, you have a gate A pipeline. That is a start, not a contract.

title: No questions before the first demo: how agents made us move our product engineering handoff
description:
I'm Abby, a growth engineer at a small startup. This year, the way work reaches me changed completely. This post covers what broke, what we changed, and the one rule that made it work.

What broke

For years our team ran on a familiar ratio: roughly one or two people in product to five engineers.

Product took an idea, researched it and shaped it in detail. Then they handed it over, and engineers finished the planning, built it and shipped it.

In February two things happened at once. Our CEO and head of product moved from London to the US, eight hours away from the engineers. And agents got good enough that product people could write real code.

That broke the ratio. By the time product had taken a customer problem, researched the options and decided on the shape of a solution, they knew enough to hand it straight to an agent and get a good result in a couple of hours. That was faster than handing it to an engineer, and they could do it at any hour, which mattered with eight time zones in the way.

Rebalance the team, or rebalance the handoff?

We had two options. We could cut engineers, or we could move the handoff.

We moved the handoff, and it was the right call.

Product now hands over an idea, not a spec. Engineers do the research, shaping and planning, then hand the build to an agent. My job changed from:

  • detailed specification → high-quality code

to:

  • ambiguous problem → high-quality code

Engineers now make many of the smaller product decisions that used to be settled long before the work reached us. Two things made that possible.

Rule: no questions before the first demo

When an engineer picks up a piece of work, they can't ask anyone anything until they've produced a demo. After that, they can talk to whoever they like, however they like.

It sounds harsh, but it does two useful things:

  1. It forces product to put what really matters into the handover. The engineer can't come back and ask, so the important context has to be written down up front.
  2. It forces the engineer to own the tradeoffs. The many small "how" decisions stop going back to product and get made by the person closest to the code.

The engineer drives instead of the product manager, and that made the whole transition much easier.

do…while vs. until

The second thing was a principle. We care a lot that engineers still do engineering. That means understanding the system we're building, and making the important tradeoffs we'll have to support later, rather than leaving them to the AI. Whether we write, or even read, every line of code matters much less.

Most AI coding tools we tried work like a do…while loop:

do {
  agent.decide();
  agent.write();
} while (!looksDone());
// ...and now you reverse-engineer its decisions from the diff

The agent makes all the decisions, and you're left trying to understand them afterwards.

We wanted an until loop instead:

const decisions = humans.decide();   // the interesting part
until (code.matches(decisions)) {
  agent.build();
}

Humans make the interesting decisions, and the agent loops until the code matches them.

Until

That loop became the product we're building, called Until. It's a Git-backed, plan-driven workflow for you and your coding agents:

  1. Plan: you and your agent draft the outcome, the approach, and what's out of scope.
  2. Review: a teammate approves the plan or sends it back with comments. This is where your attention goes, because it's where the decisions are.
  3. Build: approval releases the plan as jobs. Agents claim them, leave handoff notes as they go, and ask you when a decision is yours to make.
  4. Check: an agent review compares the code with the approved plan and lists every place they differ.

It runs locally in your own Git repo, with no server, no account and no telemetry. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Amp, OpenCode, or any agent that can run a command.

We're not public yet, but you can join the waitlist, or apply for early access if you want to try it on a real project.

The long version

Dylan, our CEO, went through all of this in his DevOpsDays talk, Pull requests are dead, long live peer review:

How has your team's handoff between product and engineering changed since agents got good? And has anyone else tried a "no questions before the demo" rule? I'd love to hear how it went.

title: Three checks before you install a Claude Code skill (from a review of 783 skills)
description:
Before you install a Claude Code skill, open its SKILL.md and check three things.

  1. Does it contain real steps? A one-line stub, a pointer to another file, or unreadable ciphertext means there is nothing to install.
  2. Where does your data go? Search the file for URLs, keys and sign-up links. Calling an outside service is fine when you know about it and chose it.
  3. Would it work on your machine? Hard-coded paths, someone else's Slack channel, instructions to switch off the sandbox, or steps for getting past a site's bot checks are all reasons to skip it.

These come from a review we ran on the AgentCraft directory in November. We collected every Claude Code skill on GitHub that we had yet to list, 783 in total, and dropped 317 of them. That is about two in five.

The first check alone would have caught 128 of the 317.

Stars told us almost nothing

Quick guess: did repo stars help predict which skills got dropped?

Barely. Dropped skills came from repos with a median of 1,572 stars. Kept skills came from repos with a median of 1,643. And 220 of the 317 dropped skills live in repos with more than 1,000 stars. Popular repos often ship demos, templates and test fixtures next to their real skills, and those were a large share of what got dropped.

How the 783 were collected and reviewed

  1. Find repos. Repos linked from five large awesome lists of Claude skills, plus eleven GitHub searches on topics such as agent-skills and claude-skills: 1,888 repos.
  2. Filter. At least 100 stars, no forks, no archived repos, pushed to in the last year, and no repos that only mirror other people's skills: 1,569 repos, of which 1,414 contain at least one SKILL.md.
  3. Pick. A few skills per repo depending on stars (20 for 5,000+ stars, down to 2 for 100+), keeping the most starred copy when the same skill name shows up in several repos: 5,169 skills. 783 of them were new to the directory and came back from review in a usable form.
  4. Review. Claude Haiku read each SKILL.md, eight per call, and either filed it under one of 38 categories or dropped it with a short reason.

The review prompt drops a skill when it exfiltrates data or secrets, harvests credentials, evades bot detection, anti-fraud or platform rules, is malware or offensive hacking against others, is mainly an ad or paid-API funnel, is a placeholder, template, test fixture or near-empty file, is a personal config useful only to its author, or is sexual content.

Why the 317 were dropped

Reason Skills
Placeholder, template, demo or test fixture 108
Paid API or ad funnel 65
Only useful to its author or one project 46
Unsafe 41
Evades detection or platform rules 35
Other (thin aliases, failed auto-extraction) 14
Encrypted, so nobody can read it 6
Sexual content 2

A few examples:

  • Demo. In a repo with about 68,000 stars, one skill only runs the date command and another fetches the temperature of one fixed city. Great for learning how skills work, useless to install.
  • Paid API funnel. Seven near-identical skills each send you to sign up for the same paid transcript API and paste in a key.
  • Unsafe. One skill sends the run's context to an outside service on its own. Nine of the 41 come from two security scanners, NVIDIA SkillSpector and Cisco's skill-scanner, which keep deliberately malicious skills as test cases, including a recipe assistant whose guardrail tells the agent to add cyanide. Those are test samples doing their job. Counting their harmless fixtures too, 25 of the 317 dropped skills come from these two scanners' test folders.
  • Encrypted. Six skills from one repo are stored with git-crypt, so the SKILL.md you would install is ciphertext.

We kept 466. One was a duplicate, so 465 went into the directory.

Limits worth knowing

Each skill got one pass from one small model, reading only the first 1,800 characters of its SKILL.md.

We also got an accidental stability test. A name-matching bug sent 266 skills that were already listed through review a second time. Same prompt, same model: 257 kept, 9 dropped. Those 266 are left out of every number above.

A dropped skill also says nothing bad about its repo. Anthropic's own skills repo has a template skill that was dropped here simply because it gives an agent nothing to do.

The full write-up, the exact review prompt and a JSON file with all 317 reasons (names removed) are on the original post:

https://agentcraft.dev/en/blog/claude-code-skills-review-2026-11/

The 465 kept skills are in the AgentCraft skills directory (5,101 skills, with install commands):

https://agentcraft.dev/en/skills/

Disclosure: I'm Adrian Vale and I help run AgentCraft.

title: Oumi's FAiE Wants to Be the Engineer That Builds Your AI Agents — Explained Honestly
description:
Building an AI agent is easy. Making one reliable enough to trust with real work is not — and that gap is exactly where Oumi, a Seattle enterprise AI platform, is aiming its new launch. Announced 4 November 2026, Oumi says it now offers end-to-end, AI-automated agent development: one platform where agents are built, evaluated, trained, deployed, monitored and continuously improved, with an AI engineer called FAiE (Frontier AI Engineer) doing much of the engineering work in between.

Oumi's framing is that enterprises should stop "renting generic intelligence" from frontier providers and instead own specialised intelligence — models trained on their own agents' work, improving over time. That is Oumi's claim, and this article labels it as such throughout. No prices, benchmarks, trial terms or hands-on results were given, and none are invented here.

What it is

At the centre is FAiE, Oumi's AI agent that automates AI engineering. Oumi says FAiE helps define objectives, design evaluations, analyse failures, curate data, select models and training strategies, and execute experiments. Extended to agent development, it also helps define tools and environments and systematically trains the models behind agents.

The workflow Oumi describes is a loop: a team describes what it wants its agents to accomplish; FAiE automates the engineering work; agents are evaluated; failures are diagnosed; and production interactions become evaluation sets and training data that improve the models powering the agents. CEO and co-founder Manos Koukoumidis: "Building AI agents is easy. Making them reliable is the next frontier... The best agents won't just rely on better prompts, expanded harnesses, or bigger generic models. They'll improve by training the weights of the models powering them, learning from their own work: where they failed, what users preferred, and whether they completed the task."

That diagnosis is the most interesting part of the announcement. When an agent fails, the cause could sit in the prompt, the tools, the orchestration, or the underlying model — and most teams today can only tune the first three. Training the model weights behind an agent has required specialised expertise and significant effort. Oumi's bet is that automating that step turns a demo agent into a dependable one.

What's new in this launch

  • End-to-end agent development in one platform. Build, evaluate, train, deploy, monitor and continuously improve agents in one place, with production failures feeding back into evaluation sets and training data.
  • Bring Your Own Harness. The most practical part for teams with agents already in production: Oumi says customers keep their existing orchestration, tools, memory, environments and application logic, and connect to Oumi for evaluation and model training — improving models within the environments where their agents already operate, rather than rebuilding on Oumi's stack.
  • Advanced post-training: DPO and GRPO. Building on existing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Oumi introduces direct preference optimisation (DPO) for preferred behaviours, and reinforcement learning through GRPO (group relative policy optimisation) against task outcomes. GRPO is in Private Preview — access by contacting Oumi, not self-serve sign-up. FAiE, Oumi says, helps select strategies, design rewards, monitor training and diagnose problems. Multi-stage training chains different methods together.

This is an extension of FAiE and the Oumi platform, not a brand-new product line.

The vendor claims — labelled as the vendor's

Every capability claim here — FAiE's automation, Bring Your Own Harness preserving existing stacks, higher quality, lower cost and greater control, agents' experiences compounding into proprietary intelligence — comes from Oumi's announcement. We have not used the platform, tested FAiE, or verified any of it hands-on.

What was not given: no price, tier or pricing model; no benchmarks, accuracy figures, reliability improvements or case-study results; no leaderboard claim (none is repeated here); no beta or trial terms beyond GRPO's Private Preview; no availability date beyond the announcement itself (4 November 2026).

Who it matters for

  • Enterprise teams whose agents work but are not reliable enough. Bring Your Own Harness is the part to interrogate first: how much of your existing stack genuinely stays untouched?
  • AI platform and ML engineering teams. FAiE is a second-order use of agents — agents building agents. Whether that automation is trustworthy is the question that decides whether this category matters.
  • Teams already invested in an agent harness. The launch's most concrete promise is that you do not abandon your orchestration, tools and memory to use Oumi's evaluation and training — a claim testable in a pilot.
  • Anyone watching the "own vs rent" debate in enterprise AI. Specialised models you own, trained on your agents' own work, versus generic frontier models — a framing that resonates on differentiation and control, and is also, plainly, a vendor's positioning.

The limits, stated plainly

No hands-on testing was performed; everything comes from Oumi's 4 November 2026 BusinessWire announcement, checked the same day.

  • All capability claims are Oumi's, unverified by us.
  • No pricing exists to report, because none was given.
  • GRPO is in Private Preview only, via contacting Oumi.
  • No performance evidence was published — "higher quality, lower cost, greater control" is Oumi's aspiration, not a reported result.
  • "Owning specialised intelligence" is a strategy, not a guarantee: training on your agents' work can compound bad data or narrow behaviour too. The announcement does not address those risks.
  • Bring Your Own Harness compatibility is described, not demonstrated.

The bottom line: Oumi's FAiE launch names a real problem — agents that work in demos and fail in production because nobody trained the model behind them — and proposes an interesting loop: evaluate, diagnose, turn failures into training data, and let an AI engineer run the cycle. But a launch with no prices, no benchmarks and no hands-on evidence is a claim about a direction, not proof of a destination. Ask Oumi for a before-and-after reliability figure on a real enterprise agent, what Bring Your Own Harness actually preserves, and what it costs. Until then, treat FAiE as a credible idea from a team of former Google Gemini engineering leaders, backed by Venrock, Obvious Ventures, Plug & Play, Mozilla Ventures and Ascend — and as an unproven product.

Sources: BusinessWire, 4 November 2026, "Oumi Launches the Agent That Builds, Trains, and Continuously Improves AI Agents" (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261104154139/en/Oumi-Launches-the-Agent-That-Builds-Trains-and-Continuously-Improves-AI-Agents); Oumi (https://oumi.ai). All capability, quality, cost and control claims are Oumi's own, not independently tested results. No hands-on testing was performed. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post, and it contains no affiliate links.

title: Agent memory architecture
description:
Agent Memory Architecture – A Practical Guide

📋 Concise Diagnosis Table

Symptom / Error Likely Root Cause Immediate Mitigation Long‑Term Remedy
Stale exchange‑rate quoted after a few seconds Working memory TTL too long or missing freshness check Force a refresh from the live rates API for any request older than RATE_TTL Implement a hard TTL per volatile data type and audit policy
User‑data remains after “Delete my data” request Durable preferences not version‑tracked or deletion path missing Run a purge script that deletes all preference keys matching the user ID and logs the action Enforce immutable audit trails for deletions and integrate privacy‑by‑design hooks
Memory‑related latency spikes during high traffic Episodic logger writes synchronously to a single store Switch episodic writes to an async queue, keep a bounded buffer Deploy a sharded write‑ahead log with back‑pressure handling
Incorrect regulatory rule applied Authoritative fact cache not refreshed before rule evaluation Bypass cache and call the compliance API for rule‑type queries Set deterministic freshness checks (e.g., MAX_AGE = 5 min) and unit‑test rule‑generation pipelines

⚠️ Editorial Caveats

  • A symptom does not prove a specific root cause; systematic investigation (labels, context, preprocessing, base‑model limits) is required before attributing errors to pre‑training or fine‑tuning.
  • Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) improves information access but does not guarantee factual accuracy, instant compliance, or complete coverage.
  • Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes base weights and learns low‑rank updates; it does not guarantee preservation of all existing behavior. Regression testing outside the target task is essential.
  • Document retrieval and live‑value API calls are distinct; cached documents must never replace a required live‑value fetch.

🧭 Decision Flow (Mermaid) 

flowchart TD
    A["Incoming request"]
    B["Is request for volatile data?"]
    C["Use Working Memory"]
    D["Is request for user preferences?"]
    E["Use Durable Preferences"]
    F["Is request for audit trace?"]
    G["Use Episodic Memory"]
    H["Is request for verified fact?"]
    I["Use Authoritative Facts"]
    A --> B
    B -->|yes| C
    B -->|no| D
    D -->|yes| E
    D -->|no| F
    F -->|yes| G
    F -->|no| H
    H -->|yes| I
    H -->|no| C

🏗️ Layer‑by‑Layer Responsibilities

Layer Primary Role Data Lifetime Access Pattern Typical TTL / Versioning
Working Memory Short‑lived context for the active session (e.g., recent user utterances, temporary calculations). Cleared after the session or after a short TTL (seconds‑to‑minutes). In‑process read/write; no persistence. SESSION_TTL = 5 min (configurable).
Durable Preferences Long‑term, mutable settings that survive sessions (e.g., preferred language, notification opt‑ins). Persisted indefinitely but versioned; can be deleted on request. Indexed look‑up, atomic updates. Version number ↑ on each change; soft‑delete flag.
Episodic Memory Immutable audit trail of actions, decisions, and tool calls (for compliance, debugging, analytics). Append‑only; retained until a pruning policy runs. Write‑only during execution; read‑only for analytics. Retention window MAX_EPISODE_AGE = 90 days (subject to regulation).
Authoritative Facts Verified data from signed knowledge bases or live APIs (e.g., tax rates, regulatory limits). Cached only as a performance shortcut; source is authoritative. Retrieval followed by deterministic freshness validation; fallback to live API guaranteed. Cache MAX_FRESHNESS = 5 min for volatile facts; indefinite for static signed docs.

Key principles

  1. TTL enforcement – each layer has a hard expiration enforced by the runtime, never by “best‑effort”.
  2. Deletion & privacy – Durable Preferences and Episodic records must support explicit user‑initiated deletion workflows that are auditable.
  3. Staleness guardrails – Authoritative Facts must never be served beyond their freshness window; a deterministic check (now - cached_at < MAX_FRESHNESS) decides whether to use the cache or hit the live source.

🛠️ Python Decision Helper (Teaching‑Only) 

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""Memory layer dispatcher – teaching only.

The helper decides which memory store a request should hit based on
metadata that the orchestration layer supplies.  It contains only
standard‑library constructs and heavy assertions to illustrate the
contract between the caller and each memory layer.
"""

import datetime as _dt
from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import NamedTuple, Literal

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class MemoryLayer(Enum):
    """Enumerates the four memory layers."""
    WORKING = auto()
    DURABLE = auto()
    EPISODIC = auto()
    AUTHORITATIVE = auto()

class Request(NamedTuple):
    """A minimal request description used by the dispatcher."""
    kind: Literal["volatile", "preference", "audit", "fact"]
    created_at: _dt.datetime  # UTC timestamp of request arrival
    ttl_seconds: int | None = None  # Optional explicit TTL

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def select_layer(req: Request) -> MemoryLayer:
    """Return the appropriate MemoryLayer for *req*.

    Assertions act as guard rails – they fail fast if the caller supplies
    contradictory information, which mirrors the deterministic business
    rules required in production.
    """
    now = _dt.datetime.utcnow()
    age = (now - req.created_at).total_seconds()

    # 1️⃣ Volatile data → Working Memory (must respect TTL)
    if req.kind == "volatile":
        assert req.ttl_seconds is not None, "TTL required for volatile data"
        assert age <= req.ttl_seconds, "Request exceeds its TTL"
        return MemoryLayer.WORKING

    # 2️⃣ User preference → Durable Preferences (no TTL, versioned)
    if req.kind == "preference":
        assert req.ttl_seconds is None, "TTL must not be set for preferences"
        return MemoryLayer.DURABLE

    # 3️⃣ Audit trail entry → Episodic Memory (append‑only)
    if req.kind == "audit":
        assert req.ttl_seconds is None, "TTL not applicable to audit logs"
        return MemoryLayer.EPISODIC

    # 4️⃣ Verified fact → Authoritative Facts (freshness check)
    if req.kind == "fact":
        # Example: allow cache only if less than 5 min old
        MAX_FRESHNESS = 300
        assert age <= MAX_FRESHNESS, "Cached fact is stale – fetch live"
        return MemoryLayer.AUTHORITATIVE

    raise ValueError(f"Unsupported request kind: {req.kind}")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example (not executed in production):
if __name__ == "__main__":
    r = Request(kind="volatile", created_at=_dt.datetime.utcnow(), ttl_seconds=30)
    assert select_layer(r) == MemoryLayer.WORKING

📜 Illustrative Architecture Decision Records

ADR 001 – Separate Working Memory from Durable Preferences

Context

Early prototypes stored both session‑level variables and user‑level settings in a single key‑value map. Privacy audits revealed that “delete my data” requests inadvertently left preference remnants, and latency spikes occurred because volatile data crowded the persistent store.

Decision

Introduce a distinct Working Memory store scoped to a session, backed by an in‑process LRU with a hard TTL (SESSION_TTL). Move all user‑level settings into Durable Preferences, persisted in a versioned KV table with an explicit deletion API.

Consequences

Positive Negative
Faster per‑turn look‑ups (no I/O) Additional serialization code for hand‑off between layers
Clear privacy boundary – deletion only touches Durable store Slightly larger memory footprint per active session

Acceptance Criteria

  • All “delete my data” automated tests verify that after the API call, no keys remain in the Durable store for the user.
  • End‑to‑end latency for a 10‑turn conversation drops ≤ 15 % in load tests.

Uncertainty – The exact TTL value may need tuning based on observed session lengths; monitoring will guide adjustments.

ADR 002 – Cache Authoritative Facts Only When Freshness Is Proven

Context

The bot frequently queried a live tax‑rate service. To improve responsiveness, a naive cache without expiry was introduced, leading to regulatory violations when rates changed.

Decision

Implement a Authoritative Facts cache that stores the raw response together with cached_at. Every read must run a deterministic freshness predicate (now - cached_at < MAX_FRESHNESS). If the predicate fails, the system must invoke the live API; fallback to cache is prohibited.

Consequences

Positive Negative
Guarantees compliance window (no stale rates beyond 5 min) Extra latency on cache miss (must call live API)
Simpler audit – every fact entry records its source timestamp Need to monitor cache hit‑rate to avoid overload of external service

Acceptance Criteria

  • In integration tests, any simulated rate change after MAX_FRESHNESS must result in a different value being returned.
  • Production monitoring shows > 95 % cache‑hit rate while never serving a fact older than MAX_FRESHNESS.

Uncertainty – External service latency variance may affect overall response time; adaptive back‑off strategies will be evaluated if miss latency exceeds a defined threshold.

✅ Evaluation & Maintenance Checklist

  • [ ] TTL Enforcement – Unit tests verify that select_layer raises on expired volatile requests.
  • [ ] Privacy Deletion – Automated job runs nightly to confirm no residual keys for users who invoked the deletion endpoint.
  • [ ] Episodic Pruning – Scheduled job trims records older than MAX_EPISODE_AGE; post‑run count must be ≤ target retention size.
  • [ ] Authoritative Freshness – Integration test injects a stale cache entry; request must trigger a live API call (mocked).
  • [ ] Performance Regression – Benchmark end‑to‑end latency before and after layer separation; reject changes that increase 95th‑percentile latency by > 10 %.
  • [ ] Regression Suite – Include prompts that require context retrieval, live‑value calls, and deterministic business‑rule evaluation; verify no drift after any code change.
  • [ ] Documentation Sync – Ensure the mermaid diagram, table definitions, and ADRs are version‑controlled alongside code.

📚 References

  1. Microsoft Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) concepts – https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/concepts/retrieval-augmented-generation
  2. LoRA: Low‑Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models – https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685

title: Proving What AI Generates: Running Formally Verified Lean 4 Inside Clojure Services
description:
TL;DR:

  • Unit tests only check sample points; formal verification in Lean 4 mathematically guarantees logic for all inputs.
  • The new Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm:0.2.615) lets you compile Lean into an intermediate artifact (.leanjvm) and interpret it directly on standard OpenJDK 17+ with zero native C/JNI dependencies.
  • This article demonstrates how an AI coding agent can write financial ledger invariants, self-correct via Lean compiler proofs, and deploy proved code into a Clojure service.

Credit & Attribution: This workflow builds on the breakthrough work by the Simmis team introducing the Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm). The financial settlement walkthrough below illustrates these mechanics applied to autonomous agent engineering.

The LLM Reliability Wall in Production

Every engineering team deploying autonomous AI coding agents eventually runs into the LLM Reliability Wall.

An agent prompted to generate an account transfer or settlement routine writes clean code in seconds. It even produces dozens of passing unit tests. But unit tests only sample finite scenarios. In financial ledgers, the bug that triggers insolvency is never the one tested by a handful of mock transactions—it lurks in the untested corner case where an overdraft limit, a currency conversion edge, and a zero-sum constraint collide.

For decades, formal methods offered the mathematical antidote: prove that code satisfies invariants for all possible inputs using proof assistants like Lean 4. But Lean code was traditionally an island:

  • Native binaries required brittle JNI or Panama bridges.
  • Memory models clashed: Lean frees memory via reference counting, while the JVM uses a garbage collector. Cycles across the boundary leak memory.
  • Deployed servers required the full native Lean toolchain installed.

The release of the Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm:0.2.615) changes this equation. It provides a pure JVM intermediate-representation (IR) interpreter that runs proved Lean functions directly on stock OpenJDK 17+.

This unlocks an autonomous ground-truth loop: agents synthesize formally verified invariants in Lean, prove them against the Lean compiler, and deploy them directly into production Clojure and Java microservices.

The Architecture: Build-Time Proofs, Run-Time JVM 

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   BUILD & PROOF STAGE                  │
│               (Linux x86-64 / CI / Docker)             │
│                                                        │
│  AI Agent writes:                                      │
│  • Settlement logic                                    │
│  • Invariant theorems (Conservation & Solvency)        │
│                                                        │
│                     ▼                                  │
│         Lean 4.33.1 Toolchain Check                    │
│    [ Fails: Agent self-corrects proof ]                │
│    [ Passes: Proof erased, IR compiled ]               │
│                     ▼                                  │
│            ledger.leanjvm Artifact                     │
│          + SHA-256 Manifest Fingerprint                │
└────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   PRODUCTION STAGE                     │
│              (Any OpenJDK 17+ Environment)             │
│                                                        │
│  Clojure / JVM Microservice                            │
│  • Loads ledger.leanjvm into pure Java Interpreter     │
│  • Zero native C / JNI / platform dependencies         │
│  • Managed 100% by JVM Garbage Collector               │
│  • Enforces instruction budgets (default: 2M ops)      │
│  • Exposes bidirectional host callbacks (IO)           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The division of labor is clean:

  1. At build time, native Lean compiles the source, checks the proofs, and strips them away. The compiler packages the intermediate code, types, and layouts into a portable .leanjvm artifact.
  2. At run time, standard Clojure services interpret the intermediate representation. The production container needs no Lean toolchain.

The Domain: A Conservation-of-Value Financial Settlement

Consider an account settlement function. The business requires two non-negotiable invariants:

  1. Solvency: No account may be debited below its configured floor (zero).
  2. Conservation of Value: The total amount debited must equal the total amount credited. No money appears or vanishes.

Let's see how an autonomous agent interacts with this system.

1. The Agent Self-Correction Loop

When an AI agent is instructed to write settlement logic, it often generates subtle bugs. Here is what happens when Lean's type checker acts as the agent's supervisor.

Round 1: The Agent Hallucinates an Edge Case

The agent drafts an initial version in Ledger.lean:

namespace Ledger

def transfer (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) : (Nat × Nat) :=
  -- Naive transfer: subtracts without checking if balance < amount
  (fromBal - amount, toBal + amount)

theorem transfer_conserves_value (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, t) := transfer fromBal toBal amount
  f + t = fromBal + toBal := by
  unfold transfer
  -- Proof attempt fails when amount > fromBal due to Nat underflow truncation!

In Lean, natural numbers (Nat) truncate subtraction at zero (3 - 5 = 0). Because of this, fromBal - amount breaks conservation of value whenever amount > fromBal!

The Lean compiler rejects the code:

error: unsolved goals
case h
fromBal toBal amount : Nat
⊢ (fromBal - amount) + (toBal + amount) = fromBal + toBal

The agent cannot hallucinate or hand-wave this failure away. The build stops cold.

Round 2: Self-Correction with Machine-Checked Solvency

The agent reads the compiler error, realizes Nat subtraction truncates at zero, and refines the logic to guard the transfer:

namespace Ledger

def settleTransfer (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) : (Nat × Nat) :=
  if amount ≤ fromBal then
    (fromBal - amount, toBal + amount)
  else
    (fromBal, toBal) -- Rejected transfer preserves balances unchanged

/-- Theorem: Transfers strictly conserve total capital. -/
theorem settle_conserves_value (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, t) := settleTransfer fromBal toBal amount
  f + t = fromBal + toBal := by
  unfold settleTransfer
  split
  · rename_i h
    omega
  · rfl

/-- Theorem: The sender account never drops below zero (solvency guarantee). -/
theorem settle_preserves_solvency (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, _) := settleTransfer fromBal toBal amount
  f ≤ fromBal := by
  unfold settleTransfer
  split
  · rename_i h
    omega
  · rfl

end Ledger

Both proofs pass. Lean guarantees that no transaction can ever violate solvency or fabricate currency, across all infinite combinations of Nat.

2. Compiling the Verified Artifact

During the CI build (currently supported on Linux x86-64 with prlimit, or via Docker), the agent triggers artifact preparation:

java -cp "$SDK_CLASSPATH" ansatz.lean.jvm.LeanPreparation \
  --source ./ledger \
  --sysroot "$LEAN_SYSROOT" \
  --producer-bundle "$PRODUCER_BUNDLE" \
  --cache "$COMPILER_CACHE" \
  --root-module Ledger \
  --entry Ledger.settleTransfer \
  --output ./ledger.leanjvm

This generates ledger.leanjvm and prints its SHA-256 fingerprint:
sha256:d8a2...3f10

3. Running Inside Clojure at the REPL

In the production service, add the SDK dependency to deps.edn:

{:deps {org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm {:mvn/version "0.2.615"}}}

Load the artifact and invoke the formally proved function directly from the Clojure REPL:

(ns ledger.core
  (:require [ansatz.lean.jvm :as lean]
            [clojure.java.io :as io]))

(defn run-settlement []
  (with-open [runtime (lean/open)
              input   (io/input-stream "ledger.leanjvm")
              project (lean/load-artifact runtime input (System/getenv "EXPECTED_MANIFEST_SHA256"))]
    (let [settle (lean/function project "Ledger.settleTransfer")]
      ;; 1. Valid transfer: $500 from Acc1 ($10,000) to Acc2 ($1,000)
      ;; 2. Overdraft attempt: $15,000 from Acc1 ($10,000) to Acc2 ($1,000)
      {:valid-transfer     (settle 10000 1000 500)
       :overdraft-rejected (settle 10000 1000 15000)})))

;; (run-settlement)
;; => {:valid-transfer     [9500N 1500N]
;;     :overdraft-rejected [10000N 1000N]}

Key runtime observations:

  • Clojure passes standard numbers and receives back persistent vectors containing java.math.BigInteger instances.
  • Zero JNI code or platform native bridges.
  • Memory management is 100% handled by the JVM garbage collector.

4. Inversion of Control: Lean Calling Clojure

Real business operations require dynamic runtime data—like querying fee tiers from a database or configuration file.

Lean declares the external callback:

namespace Ledger

@[extern "ansatz_jvm_account_fee"]
opaque getAccountFee : String → IO Nat

def settleWithFee (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) (tier : String) : IO (Nat × Nat) := do
  let feeRate ← getAccountFee tier
  let fee := (amount * feeRate) / 1000
  let totalDebit := amount + fee
  if totalDebit ≤ fromBal then
    pure (fromBal - totalDebit, toBal + amount)
  else
    pure (fromBal, toBal)

end Ledger

In Clojure, supply the implementation under the declaration's name when loading the artifact:

(def host-bindings
  {"Ledger.getAccountFee"
   {:implementation-id "fees/v1"
    :effect :io
    :fn (fn [tier]
          (case tier
            "vip"      0N     ;; Zero fee
            "standard" 15N    ;; 1.5% fee
            50N))}})          ;; Default 5.0%

(with-open [runtime (lean/open)
              input   (io/input-stream "ledger.leanjvm")
              project (lean/load-artifact runtime input 
                                          (System/getenv "EXPECTED_MANIFEST_SHA256")
                                          host-bindings)]
  ;; IO functions return an IOResult object carrying values or errors
  (let [result (lean/call project "Ledger.settleWithFee" 10000 1000 2000 "standard")]
    (if (.isOk result)
      (.getValue result)
      (throw (ex-info "Lean IO Error" {:cause (.getError result)})))))
;; => [7970N 3000N]  ; Total debit: 2000 + 30 fee = 2030

Mathematical proofs that parameterize over host inputs remain sound, even when values are resolved dynamically by host Clojure code.

5. Architectural Differentiator: Forkable Execution State

Why run Lean through a pure JVM interpreter instead of compiling hot machine code?

The Simmis team highlighted an architectural breakthrough: execution state forkability.

Because Lean's entire execution state (call frames, heap objects, and registers) is stored as standard JVM heap objects, the engine can clone that state mid-computation. Pausing an engine allows branching it into two independent engines that proceed down separate computational paths.

Note: While the core Ansatz engine implements state forking internally today, the public SDK does not expose fork handles yet. It represents groundwork for upcoming releases.

For future AI reasoning pipelines, this capability enables:

  • Counterfactual Branching: An agent pauses a complex financial settlement, branches the execution into two what-if paths (e.g., assessing different liquidity routing strategies), and compares the outcomes.
  • Rollback without Transaction Resets: Discarding a failed branch requires only dropping the cloned JVM object, with zero external database rollback needed.

6. Safety & Operational Guardrails

When executing autonomous agent code in production, defensive constraints are mandatory:

Guardrail Enforcement Mechanism
Infinite Recursion / DOS Invocations run under strict instruction budgets (default: 2,000,000 steps) and wall-clock timeouts (default: 5.0s).
Tampered / Stale Artifacts Artifact loading strictly validates the build-time SHA-256 manifest hash before execution.
Error Isolation Out-of-budget calls fail cleanly with ProjectFailed. The service restarts the engine via project.restart(), discarding corrupted state while preserving verified code handles.
Language Constraints The current release enforces closed, first-order signatures across host boundaries and caps project modules at 128 (beyond Lean's Init).

Conclusion

The conversation around AI coding agents has focused primarily on generating code and generating unit tests. But in high-consequence domains like finance, tests cannot establish absolute correctness.

By uniting Lean 4's proof assistant with the JVM's operational maturity, tools like Ansatz establish a practical verification bridge:

  1. Agents specify and prove invariants rather than guessing implementations.
  2. The compiler enforces ground truth, rejecting flawed edge cases with actionable counter-examples.
  3. The runtime executes natively on standard JVMs, eliminating native operational overhead.

The future of autonomous systems isn't just agents that code faster—it's agents that prove their work before hitting production.

Further Reading

  • Primary Source: Simmis: Lean on the JVM: proved functions for Java and Clojure
  • SDK Artifact: org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm on Clojars
  • Lean 4 Guide: Functional Programming in Lean by David Thrane Christiansen

description:

Security

  • Claude Code issue: email address sent to websites: A GitHub issue reporting that Claude Code passes the user's email address to sites it contacts drew heavy discussion on Hacker News. Worth reading if you use agentic tools with account-linked identity. GitHub issue

AI & tooling
